title: train_conformal_model builds every base estimator from an EMPTY parameter dict — the exact library-default defect model_defaults.py exists to prevent
what_the_code_does: On the default path the `else:` branch sets only `predictor_type = 'split'` and `params_source = 'default'`; `params` stays `{}`. It then calls `RandomForestRegressor(random_state=iteration_seed, **params)`, `XGBRegressor(random_state=iteration_seed, **params)`, `RandomForestQuantileRegressor(random_state=iteration_seed, **params)`. `sklearn_params(...)` is never called anywhere in this function — unlike train_rf_model:1380, train_xgboost_model:1619, train_lgb_model:1661.
consequence: conformal_rf gets sklearn's max_features=1.0 instead of the spec's 0.3; conformal_qrf gets 100 trees instead of 300; conformal_xgboost gets the booster's learning_rate 0.3 instead of 0.1 — which model_defaults.py:89-91 records as costing up to 0.05 R-squared under injected noise. The conformal models are therefore NOT wrappers around the same base models they are compared against, and the 'conformal rho > 0.99 with rf' justification for excluding them rests on a different forest.
source: QM9 model construction — parameter paths, shared-defaults wiring, train/val handling, Bayesian transformations (models/models.py)

title: BNN-Full and BNN-Last (torchbnn) are trained with plain MSE — no KL/ELBO term exists anywhere in the file
what_the_code_does: `criterion` is replaced by `VBLLLoss` only for `"variational"` and `"full_variational"`. For `"full"` (and `"last_layer"`) the criterion set at 2159/2802 by `get_loss_function('mse')` is left in place. A grep for `BKLLoss`, `kl_loss`, `kl_weight` across models.py returns nothing. torchbnn's BayesLinear.forward (site-packages/torchbnn/modules/linear.py:79-97) samples weights through the reparameterisation trick in both train and eval mode, so `weight_log_sigma` receives MSE gradients.
consequence: The variational posterior width is an unregularised free parameter that MSE drives toward zero; prior_sigma=0.1 acts only as an initialisation (set by reset_parameters at linear.py:54). The 'epistemic uncertainty' reported for BNN-alpha/BNN-beta is whatever residual weight noise the fit happened to leave, not a posterior. The VBLL variants, which DO carry a KL term (VBLLLoss at models.py:1238-1249), are therefore not comparable to them on equal footing.
source: QM9 model construction — parameter paths, shared-defaults wiring, train/val handling, Bayesian transformations (models/models.py)

title: train_bnn_last_standalone is labelled mlp_bnn_last but builds the DNN topology, and keeps the last epoch rather than the best
what_the_code_does: The model is `nn.Sequential(Linear(d,128), ReLU, Dropout(0.2), Linear(128,64), ReLU, Dropout(0.2), BayesLinear(64,1))` — 128 then 64, which is NEURAL_DEFAULTS['dnn']['hidden_sizes']. NEURAL_DEFAULTS['mlp'] is hidden_size 128 with num_hidden_layers 2, i.e. 128 then 128. Results are saved as 'mlp_bnn_last'. Its own early-stopping loop tracks `best_val_loss` and a patience counter but never snapshots or restores weights, so it returns whatever epoch the counter stopped on. It reads nothing from model_defaults: 128/64, dropout 0.2, lr 0.001, batch 32, patience 10, `range(100)`, prior_sigma 0.1 and n_samples 100 are all literals, and `iteration_seed` is accepted but never used to seed anything.
consequence: A results row named for NN-beta contains NN-alpha's network. It is also the one neural function still carrying the defect train_nn:1902-1920 was rewritten to fix (up to 10 epochs past the validation optimum, spent memorising corrupted labels), so its degradation curve is steeper for a procedural reason. Reachable only via model_type 'mlp_bnn_last_standalone' (process_and_train.py:1586), which no job script requests.
source: QM9 model construction — parameter paths, shared-defaults wiring, train/val handling, Bayesian transformations (models/models.py)

title: train_gnn has no early stopping and ignores args.epochs — it always trains a full 100 epochs on noisy labels
what_the_code_does: `for epoch in range(100):` with no validation loss computed inside the loop and no break. `val_loader` is used only later (3296-3315) to fit a temperature. `args.epochs` (default 100, CLI-settable) is never read. train_nn, by contrast, early-stops with patience 10 and restores the best epoch's weights (models.py:1920, 1955-1957, 2010-2020).
consequence: The GNN fits corrupted labels for the full budget while DNN/MLP/flexible_dnn roll back to their validation optimum. Any comparison of GNN robustness against the tabular neural models is confounded by the stopping rule, in the direction that makes the GNN look less robust.
source: QM9 model construction — parameter paths, shared-defaults wiring, train/val handling, Bayesian transformations (models/models.py)

title: create_gnn_model is defined four times; only the last definition is live, and it is not the architecture the module-level GCN/GAT/GIN classes describe
line: 418, 3114, 3170, 3588 (live); class GCN also defined twice, at 240 and 285
what_the_code_does: Python binds the last definition at import, so `create_gnn_model` at models.py:3588 is the one train_gnn:3231 calls. That factory defines a local `GNNRegressor` with GCNConv/GATConv/GINConv stacks, dropout between conv layers and `global_mean_pool` — and no batch normalisation. The earlier factory at :418 returns the module-level GCN (285), GAT (321) and GIN (365) classes, which are consequently unreachable, as is the first `class GCN` at :240. `pyg_to_grakel` is likewise defined twice (3367, 3552).
consequence: Three GNN architectures sit in the file looking authoritative and never run. Anyone reading the class definitions to describe the GNN in the paper describes a model that was never trained. No numeric effect on what runs today, but it is precisely the identity-error shape this codebase has been bitten by.

title: --calibration-size is accepted, passed down, and never used: conformal calibrates on the whole validation set
what_the_code_does: `train_conformal_model(..., calibration_size, ...)` takes the argument (passed from process_and_train.py:1503 as args.calibration_size, default 20, documented as a percentage) and the function body never references it — grep for `calibration_size` in models.py finds it only in the two conformal signatures and at 7391 in an unrelated function. Conformity scores are computed as `np.abs(y_val - y_val_pred)` over all of x_val.
consequence: The advertised 20% calibration carve-out does not happen; 100% of validation is the calibration set. Conformal interval widths and coverage are computed on five times the intended number of calibration points, and the remaining 80% is never used for anything.

title: Three different training-set compositions across models, none of them recorded in model_defaults
what_the_code_does: rf/qrf (1391), svm (1464), xgboost (1623) and lgb (1665) do `x_train = np.vstack((x_train, x_val))` unconditionally — all of validation goes into training. ngboost (1506) and gauche (1815) stack only `x_val[:len(x_val)//2]` when `args.uncertainty` is true, holding the other half for temperature calibration. dnn/mlp/flexible_dnn never stack: x_train alone builds the train_loader and x_val (or its first half when Bayesian+uncertainty) is the validation set for early stopping. The QM9 job scripts pass `-u True` for ngboost, qrf, gauche and gauche_rbf.
consequence: Under the standard split, the tree/kernel models train on ~11% more molecules than the neural models, and ngboost/gauche on ~5.5% more. The ANOVA's model factor therefore confounds model family with training-set size. model_defaults.py pins parameters but says nothing about this, so the parity audit cannot see it.

title: Optuna-suggested values that are computed and then discarded
line: 1386 and 1397 (qrf quantile); 3652 and 3689 (conformal alpha); 3653 and 3690 (conformal predictor_type); 2066-2091 and 2156 (dnn loss hyperparameters)
what_the_code_does: (a) `quantile = trial.suggest_float('quantile', 0.1, 0.9) if args.tuning else 0.5` at 1386 is stored only via `trial.set_user_attr`; prediction at 1397 uses hard-coded `quantiles=[0.16, 0.5, 0.84]`. (b) conformal `alpha` suggested at 3652 is overwritten at 3689 by `args.alpha`. (c) conformal `predictor_type` suggested at 3653 is a local never written into `params`, so `params.pop('predictor_type', 'split')` at 3690 always returns 'split' — the ACI predictor can never be selected. (d) train_dnn_model builds loss-specific `loss_kwargs` (delta, c, gamma, alpha, quantile, alpha_init, coeff...) at 2066-2091, then line 2156 executes `loss_kwargs = {}`, discarding all of it before `get_loss_function(loss_name, **loss_kwargs)` at 2159. `loss_name` and `needs_domains` are recomputed too, with a shorter domain-loss list.
consequence: Optuna searches over four parameters that cannot affect the objective, so the tuning results for those are noise. Default-path results are unaffected (all four have the same effective value as the default), but a tuned re-run would silently ignore them.

title: gp_fit_collapsed is written and never called
line: 1716 (definition); no call site — grep finds one occurrence in the file
what_the_code_does: The function computes whether a GP's predictions vary by less than GP_DEFAULTS['collapse_fraction'] of the training label spread and prints a warning. train_gauche_model (1769-1899) never calls it; neither does train_conformal_model's gauche branch.
consequence: The guard its docstring describes ('Never let it pass silently') does not run. A collapsed GP fit still produces an R-squared near zero that reads as a bad representation rather than a failed fit — the exact misreading the newly added init_rbf_lengthscale (1679) was written to prevent. The lengthscale fix is wired in (called from fit_gp_with_fallback:1749); the collapse detector is not.

title: Seven results rows record params_source='default' by omission rather than by fact
what_the_code_does: Each of these `save_results(...)` calls stops at `metrics` and never passes the `params_source` variable the function computed a few lines earlier. scripts/utils.py:28 declares `params_source='default'` as the keyword default, so the CSV gets 'default'. train_rf_model:1432, train_ngboost_model:1561, train_dnn_model:2294, train_flexible_dnn_model:2634, train_mlp_variant_model:2903 and train_conformal_model:3895 all pass it correctly.

title: model_defaults values that models.py restates as literals instead of reading — the parity audit cannot see any of them
what_the_code_does: Every value listed is a hard-coded literal that happens to equal its NEURAL_DEFAULTS / BAYESIAN_DEFAULTS counterpart. `BAYESIAN_DEFAULTS` is imported at models.py:66 and referenced nowhere else in the file (grep confirms a single hit). `UNCERTAINTY_DEFAULTS` is imported at 67 and likewise never used — its `calibration_fraction_of_val: 0.5` is restated as `len(x_val) // 2` at 1506, 1815, 2119, 2508, 2729. `NEURAL_DEFAULTS['training']` keys `optimizer`, `weight_decay`, `epochs` and `standardise_targets` are never read either; epochs comes from args.epochs and target standardisation is done globally in Rust, not per-split on training labels as the comment at model_defaults.py claims. GP_DEFAULTS['max_train_n'] and GP_DEFAULTS['kernel'] are also never read (the kernel comes from args.kernel at models.py:1789, default 'tanimoto', not the spec's 'rbf'). Separately, process_and_train.py:1583-1585 builds the GNN loaders at batch_size=64.
consequence: Changing a number in model_defaults.py silently fails to change QM9 behaviour for all of these, while spec_version/spec_hash in every results row assert that it did. model_defaults.py rule 5 says `audit_pipeline_parity.py --strict` catches drift, but that script builds models FROM the spec — it cannot detect that models.py builds from literals instead. The spec_hash column would therefore certify a run that did not use the spec.

title: The tuned parameter path is unreachable for two reasons beyond the one recorded
what_the_code_does: `load_best_hyperparameters(model_type, rep, results_dir='results')` returns None unless BOTH `results/master_tuned_hyperparameters.json` and `results/hyperparameter_decisions.json` exist relative to the current working directory. `results/hyperparameter_decisions.json` does not exist in this repo (only master_tuned_hyperparameters.json does). The job scripts `cd scripts` before invoking python, and `scripts/results/` does not exist.
consequence: Even if a job passed --use-best-params, the tuned branch could not fire; `if not params:` falls through to the default branch and params_source is reset to 'default'. This is benign — it confirms model_defaults.py's changelog claim that the default branch is what runs — but the code silently degrades rather than saying it could not find the file it was told to use.

title: VBLLLayer.forward has identical training and eval branches
what_the_code_does: `if self.training:` and `else:` contain four textually identical statements — both sample weight and bias through the reparameterisation trick.
consequence: No behavioural effect, and the eval-time sampling is what the MC uncertainty passes need. But the branch reads as though eval does something different (e.g. use the posterior mean), which is a trap for anyone reasoning about whether VBLL point predictions are deterministic. They are not: `y_pred` for the VBLL models is the mean of 100 stochastic passes (2242-2247), while for a plain DNN it is a single deterministic pass (2273-2280).

title: Non-neural models are fitted on raw log-unit labels while QM9 fits them on z-scored labels
line: 1093-1160 (run_tree_experiment fits mdl on y_noisy with no target scaler); the only y scaler is inside train_neural_regression at 867
what_the_code_does: run_tree_experiment applies StandardScaler to X only. `mdl.fit(X_train, y_noisy)` (1148) is given the labels in their native units — log D, log efflux ratio, pKi. Target standardisation exists only in the neural path.
other_pipeline: QM9 z-scores the target for EVERY model: the Rust writer standardises property_value with the clean training mean/SD (rust/src/main.rs:1798-1800) before any model sees it, and models.py fits SVR/NGBoost/GP on that standardised y (models/models.py:1467, 1506-1511, 1815-1820).
consequence: SVR is not scale-invariant in y: the shared spec pins C=1.0 and leaves epsilon at the sklearn default 0.1 (model_defaults.py:130-134). On a standardised label (SD 1) epsilon=0.1 is a tenth of a standard deviation; on a raw label whose SD is a few tenths of a log unit it is a large dead zone, and C=1.0 is a very different amount of regularisation. The GP's spec inits (likelihood_noise 1e-3, outputscale 1.0) and NGBoost's fixed learning rate 0.01 over 500 stages are likewise defined relative to a unit-variance target on the QM9 side and to an arbitrary-variance target here. Baseline R2 and the shape of the degradation curve for SVM, GP and NGBoost differ between the pipelines for this reason alone.
source: Model construction on the experimental side (KIRBy/tests/alternative_data_noise_robustness.py): estimators in run_dataset, neural models in train_neural_regression, the GP wrapper, cross-fitting, and seeds — checked line by line against qsar_qm_models/models/model_defaults.py, models/models.py, scripts/process_and_train.py and rust/src/main.rs

title: Tree, boosting and kernel models are trained on 64% of the data here and on 90% in QM9, because the validation carve-out is never returned to them
what_the_code_does: Each outer scaffold fold gives 80% train / 20% test; run_dataset then carves the first 20% of the training rows off as validation (`n_val = len(train_idx) // 5`, 1615-1616) and hands only `X_train`/`y_train` (the remaining 64% of the dataset) to run_tree_experiment (1683-1700). The 16% validation block is used by nothing except the neural early-stopping path.
other_pipeline: QM9 stacks the validation split back onto training for every non-neural model before fitting: models/models.py:1391 (RF/QRF), 1464 (SVM), 1623 (XGBoost), 1665 (LightGBM), 1506-1511 (NGBoost), 1815-1820 (GP). With an 80/10/10 scaffold split (scripts/process_and_train.py:605) those models see 90% of the molecules.
consequence: The same named model is fitted on materially different amounts of data in the two studies (64% vs 90% of the respective dataset), and training-set size is itself a determinant of label-noise robustness — more data averages more of the injected noise away. Baseline R2 is depressed here relative to what the same estimator would give, and every cross-pipeline robustness comparison carries an uncontrolled sample-size term. This also collides with the existing supervisor query about the 'smaller datasets' claim.

title: Neural models are never seeded on the experimental side; QM9 seeds torch per repetition
line: whole file — `grep -n manual_seed` returns nothing; contrast the pinned `random_state=42` at 1507, 1512, 1520, 1525, 1530
what_the_code_does: There is no `torch.manual_seed` anywhere in the module. Weight initialisation in DeterministicRegressor/MLPRegressor/VBLLLayer and the DataLoader shuffle at 920 all draw from PyTorch's global generator, which is seeded nondeterministically at process start. Every neural fit in a job consumes that one stream in sequence, so the result for a given (model, rep, condition, level, fold) depends on how many neural fits ran before it — i.e. on how the roster was split across SLURM tasks. The file is aware of this: the out-of-fold block at 1297-1306 snapshots and restores the torch RNG state precisely because the stream is shared, but nothing pins its starting point.
other_pipeline: QM9 calls `torch.manual_seed(iteration_seed)` before each neural fit — models/models.py:2217, 2573, 2819 — and again before the stochastic prediction passes (2217 region), so a QM9 neural row is reproducible from its iteration number.
consequence: No neural row on LogD/Caco-2/hERG is reproducible, and rows produced by a `--models BNN-Full` job do not match the same cell from a full-roster job. Fold-to-fold spread for the six neural models mixes initialisation variance with data variance in an uncontrolled way, and a re-run to check a suspicious number cannot confirm or refute it. The five sklearn/boosting models have the opposite problem: `random_state=42` is pinned identically in every fold, level and condition, so their fold spread contains no model-seed variance at all, while QM9 varies `iteration_seed` per repetition (deliberate per model_defaults.py:49-50) — the two studies' error bars mean different things.

title: The noise seed is keyed on the POSITION of a level in the grid, so a --sigmas subset run does not reproduce the corresponding rows of a full run — the opposite of what the function promises
what_the_code_does: `_injector_for(condition, level_index)` builds the seed as `base*1000003 + crc32(condition) + level_index*7919` (1073). The callers pass `sigma_levels.index(sigma)` (1136, 1228, 1247) — the index of the level within whatever grid this invocation is running, not the level itself. `--sigmas` (main, 1992-1993) replaces the grid wholesale.
other_pipeline: Not applicable — the QM9 noise plan is built in Rust from the level value.
consequence: The docstring at 1060-1063 states the goal as 'a run of a subset of the grid would then not reproduce the corresponding rows of a full run', and the implementation causes exactly that: in the full LogD grid [0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0] the level 0.5 has index 3, but in a `--sigmas 0.0 0.5` job it has index 1, so the two runs inject different corruption at the same nominal level. run_dataset then splices subset-run rows into all_results.csv by model/rep mask (1866-1883), producing a file whose rows at one level came from different noise realisations. Fix: derive the seed from the level VALUE (e.g. crc32 of its repr) rather than its position.

title: The early-stopping validation split is not scaffold-disjoint from training, while QM9's is
what_the_code_does: `n_val = len(train_idx) // 5; val_idx_local = np.arange(n_val)` takes the first fifth of the outer fold's training index. GroupKFold returns train indices in ascending original order, so this is simply the lowest-numbered 20% of the training molecules — an arbitrary slice with respect to scaffold. Molecules in it routinely share Murcko scaffolds with the 64% kept for training. The file states the overlap itself, at 1284-1287: 'Reusing the outer validation set would early-stop against molecules sharing scaffolds with the rows being scored (26-42% overlap on the real datasets)'.
other_pipeline: QM9's validation split is scaffold-disjoint — deepchem ScaffoldSplitter with frac_train=0.8/frac_valid=0.1/frac_test=0.1 (scripts/process_and_train.py:605) — and its neural models early-stop on that.
consequence: The six neural models on the experimental datasets are early-stopped against an interpolation-regime validation set, while the QM9 neural models are early-stopped against an extrapolation-regime one. A validation set that shares scaffolds with training keeps improving while the network memorises, so stopping happens later and more injected noise is absorbed — which biases exactly the quantity the study measures, and only for the neural half of the roster. The inner cross-fitting path already carves its own split for this reason (1283-1290); the outer path does not.

title: gp_fit_method records only the LAST noise level's fitter and stamps it on every level; out-of-fold fallbacks are never recorded and there is no gp_collapsed column
what_the_code_does: GaussianProcessGauche.fit wraps the botorch fitter in `try/except Exception` (809-833) and on any failure runs a 100-step Adam loop, setting `self.fit_method_` to 'adam_fallback'. run_tree_experiment copies that into a single scalar, `extras['gp_fit_method'] = mdl.fit_method_` (1152), inside the per-level loop, so each level overwrites the previous one; at 1749 the surviving value is broadcast onto every sigma row of the block. The inner out-of-fold fits (1179-1181) build their own model via `model_fn()` and their fit_method_ is discarded entirely. There is no collapse check.
other_pipeline: QM9 records the fitter per fit (models/models.py fit_gp_with_fallback, called around models.py:1837) AND a `gp_collapsed` flag from gp_fit_collapsed, both written by save_results (scripts/utils.py:25,30,71).
consequence: If botorch succeeds at low noise and refuses at high noise (or vice versa) the CSV says every level used the same optimiser. A GP row that reads 'botorch' may have been produced by the Adam fallback, which is a different optimisation. Out-of-fold GP uncertainties — the input to question A — carry no fit-method provenance at all. And a GP that collapsed to a constant prediction is recorded here as a low R2 with `spearman` forced to 0.0 (compute_metrics, 1333) rather than flagged, so a failed fit is indistinguishable from a bad representation, which is the exact situation QM9 added gp_collapsed to prevent.

title: A neural fit that never improves crashes on load_state_dict(None), and the blanket except in run_dataset turns that into a silently missing cell
what_the_code_does: `best_state = None` (927) is only assigned when `vl < best_val - tolerance` (938). With tolerance = 0.0 that comparison is False for a NaN or inf validation loss, so a run that diverges on epoch 1 leaves best_state None and line 947 `model.load_state_dict(best_state)` raises TypeError. In run_dataset the whole (model, rep, condition) block is wrapped in `except Exception as e: print(f'    ERROR: {e}'); continue` (1843-1845), so the failure produces one log line and no rows.
other_pipeline: QM9's train_nn keeps `restore_best` behind the spec flag and skips restoration when there is no validation set (models/models.py train_nn, around the early-stopping block), and a failed QM9 fit ends the job rather than being swallowed.
consequence: A model/representation combination that diverges systematically — most likely on the 1024-dim MHG-GNN or 768-dim ChemBERTa vectors — vanishes from all_results.csv while the job exits 0 and the partial-checkpoint file makes it look productive. run_dataset guards only the all-cells-failed case (1855-1861). Missing cells are not missing at random, so any ANOVA or Wilcoxon over the model x rep grid is computed on a biased subset. Minimum fix: `if best_state is not None` at 947, plus a non-NaN guard, plus counting swallowed exceptions and failing the job above a threshold.

title: retention_0.5 and retention_1.0 are NaN for two of the three datasets because the anchored level grids no longer contain 0.5 or 1.0
line: 1903-1906, against NOISE_LEVELS_BY_DATASET at 169-174 and CENSORING_LEVELS at 181
what_the_code_does: The summary block selects `fold_avgs[fold_avgs['sigma'] == 0.5]` and `== 1.0` by exact float equality. The per-dataset grids are LogD [0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0], Caco-2 [0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.7] and hERG [0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.54, 0.8, 1.1]. Caco-2 has 0.5 but no 1.0; hERG has neither.
other_pipeline: Not applicable — QM9 summarises its own grid.
consequence: summary.csv and combined_summary.csv carry a retention_1.0 column that is populated for LogD only and a retention_0.5 column that is populated for LogD and Caco-2 only. Averaging or tabulating those columns across datasets silently compares one dataset against a blank, and the hERG rows contribute nothing while looking like an ordinary row. Either index by grid position (first, mid, last) or drop the columns in favour of auc_norm, which is computed over whatever grid was run.

title: The GP's likelihood noise and outputscale are hard-coded literals at the construction site, bypassing GP_DEFAULTS
what_the_code_does: `GaussianProcessGauche(kernel=k, init_noise=1e-3, init_outputscale=1.0)`. The wrapper's constructor does read GP_DEFAULTS['likelihood_noise'] and GP_DEFAULTS['outputscale'] (766-769) — but only when the argument is None, and the call site always passes a literal. The kernel likewise comes from the `--gp-kernel` CLI default 'rbf' (1994), not from GP_DEFAULTS['kernel']. Only fallback_adam_lr, fallback_adam_iters, apply_outputscale and max_train_n are genuinely read from the spec (770, 800, 823, 189).
other_pipeline: QM9 reads both from the spec in the default branch: models/models.py `params['outputscale'] = GP_DEFAULTS['outputscale']` and `params['likelihood_noise'] = GP_DEFAULTS['likelihood_noise']` (in train_gauche_model).
consequence: No number moves today — the literals equal the spec values. But this is precisely the pattern model_defaults.py exists to abolish: editing GP_DEFAULTS['likelihood_noise'] or ['outputscale'] would change QM9's GP and leave the experimental GP untouched, and the spec_hash written into both CSVs would move in lockstep, asserting a parity that no longer holds. scripts/audit_pipeline_parity.py builds only the SKLEARN_DEFAULTS estimators (_build_kwargs, line 277-287) and would not catch it.

title: BAYESIAN_DEFAULTS is imported and never used; every BNN and VBLL constant is a local literal
what_the_code_does: Line 122 binds `BAYESIAN_DEFAULTS = MODEL_SPEC.BAYESIAN_DEFAULTS` and no other line in the file references the name. The torchbnn transform hard-codes `{'prior_mu': 0, 'prior_sigma': 0.1}` at 591 (full BNN) and 612 (last-layer BNN); VBLLLayer hard-codes prior_mu=0.0/prior_sigma=1.0 (639), weight_log_sigma init -3.0 (647), bias_log_sigma init -3.0 (650) and log_noise_var init -2.0 (652).
other_pipeline: Identical situation on the QM9 side: models/models.py imports BAYESIAN_DEFAULTS (line 66) and never references it; the same six constants are literals at models.py:1079, 1123 (prior_sigma 0.1) and 1151, 1160, 1165 (VBLLLayer 1.0 / -3.0 / -2.0). I verified all six pairs match today.
consequence: No divergence right now — the four Bayesian nets are byte-for-byte the same construction in both pipelines. The risk is one-sided drift: BAYESIAN_DEFAULTS is decorative on both sides, so it is a guard that would not fire, and the spec_hash in the results rows would go on certifying a parity the spec no longer controls. Either wire both sides to the dict or delete the section from model_defaults.py so it does not read as a guarantee.

title: Several NEURAL_DEFAULTS keys are never read: epochs is hard-coded at both call sites, and restore_best_weights / standardise_targets / val_loss_reduction / optimizer / weight_decay / dnn dropout and activation are ignored
line: 1256, 1290 (epochs=100); 947 (unconditional restore); 866-872 (unconditional standardisation); 936 (whole-set mean loss); 913 (Adam, no weight_decay); 545-548 (Dropout(0.2)), 552 (ReLU)
what_the_code_does: train_neural_regression falls back to `_t['epochs']` only when the caller passes None (863), but both call sites pass `epochs=100` explicitly (1256, 1290), so the spec key is dead. `restore_best_weights` is never consulted — line 947 always restores. `standardise_targets` is never consulted — 866-872 always standardise. `val_loss_reduction` is never consulted; the code happens to satisfy 'mean' by evaluating the whole validation set in one forward pass (936). `optimizer` and `weight_decay` are not passed to torch.optim.Adam (913). DeterministicRegressor hard-codes Dropout(0.2) at 545/548 and ReLU at 546/549 rather than reading NEURAL_DEFAULTS['dnn']['dropout_rate'] / ['activation'] (only hidden_sizes is read, at 897).
other_pipeline: QM9 reads patience, tolerance, restore_best_weights and val_loss_reduction from the spec in train_nn (models/models.py train_nn, the block that begins 'Early stopping is defined once, in models/model_defaults.py'), but it too hard-codes batch_size=32 at every DataLoader (models.py:2139-2140, 2528-2529, 2755, 2964) and its DNNRegressionModel hard-codes Dropout(p=0.2) (models.py:1029) without reading dropout_rate. So restore_best_weights and val_loss_reduction are live on the QM9 side and dead here.
consequence: Flipping `restore_best_weights` to False or `val_loss_reduction` to 'sum' in model_defaults.py would change QM9's neural models and leave the experimental ones exactly as they are — a one-sided change with an identical spec_hash on both CSVs. The values agree today so no current number moves.

title: A non-RBF GP falls out of the uncertainty roster and out of the GP dispatch branch, while still being caught by the subsample guard
what_the_code_does: The GP's display name is `'GP' if gp_kernel == 'rbf' else f'GP-{gp_kernel.capitalize()}'` (1548). UNCERTAINTY_MODELS lists 'GP' only (149), so `_oof = oof_folds if model_name in UNCERTAINTY_MODELS else 0` (1679) silently disables cross-fitting for 'GP-Tanimoto'. The dispatch that routes the GP through its subsampled arrays tests `model_name == 'GP'` (1683), while the subsample block itself tests `model_name.startswith('GP')` (1642) — the two guards do not agree. Separately, the GP is only constructed for reps in gp_rep_set, which defaults to {'PDV'} (1481).
other_pipeline: QM9 names the two GP variants gauche_rbf and gauche (models.py, in train_gauche_model) and has no out-of-fold machinery, so there is no roster to match.
consequence: Answering the review question directly: with the defaults, the roster that gets cross-fitting (QRF, NGBoost, GP, BNN-Full, VBLL-Full, MLP-BNN-Full, MLP-VBLL-Full) does exactly match the roster that _tree_mean_std and train_neural_regression can produce a per-molecule uncertainty for (1033-1050, 955-963) — the match is correct today. It breaks the moment `--gp-kernel tanimoto` is used: that job produces GP uncertainties on the test split but no out-of-fold block, with no warning, and the two GP guards at 1642/1683 disagree so a future max_train_n cap would subsample the arrays and then fit on the unsubsampled ones. Also note the GP reaches cross-fitting on one representation out of six by default, so question A is answerable for the GP on PDV alone.

title: The SNS vocabulary is fitted on every molecule in the dataset, including the held-out fold — the QM9 pipeline fits it on training molecules only
what_the_code_does: generate_representations calls `create_sns(smiles_list, return_featurizer=True)` on the full SMILES array, and run_dataset calls generate_representations at line 1500 BEFORE the GroupKFold loop that first defines train_idx/test_idx (line ~1602). So the substructure prevalence counts at molecular.py:1195-1199, and therefore which 1024 substructures occupy the 1024 feature slots, are computed from the test molecules as well as the training ones. Verified empirically: create_sns on the first three of five molecules does not reproduce the first three rows of create_sns on all five.
consequence: Two problems. (a) A structure-level train/test leak in a study whose headline quantity is how performance degrades — the feature basis for every fold already knows which substructures the held-out molecules contain. It is unsupervised so the effect is modest, but it is not zero, and it is asymmetric across representations (only SNS has it). (b) It is a different protocol from QM9, so 'SNS' names two different fitting procedures as well as two different dtypes.
other_pipeline: scripts/process_and_train.py:618-622 builds `mols_train` from train_idx only and passes just those molecules to create_sort_and_slice_ecfp_featuriser; scripts/process_and_train.py:758-761 does the same on the QM9 branch. QM9 has no such leak.

title: Every representation is z-scored per fold before the model, so ECFP4 and Avalon stop being binary — and the offered `--gp-kernel tanimoto` is then computed on real-valued, sign-mixed input
what_the_code_does: Both experiment runners open with `scaler = StandardScaler(); X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train); X_test = scaler.transform(X_test)` applied unconditionally to whatever matrix they were handed. For ECFP4 and Avalon that turns {0,1} bits into centred, unit-variance real numbers: a bit set in 1 molecule of N leaves the other N-1 at about -1/sqrt(N) and that one at about +sqrt(N). Meanwhile GaussianProcessGauche._kernel_class (line 780-788) offers TanimotoKernel, the CLI advertises it at line ~1996 as 'only valid on binary fingerprints (ECFP4)', and the experiment comment at line ~1546 repeats that.
consequence: For RF/XGBoost/LightGBM/QRF nothing changes (monotone per-feature transform). For SVM-RBF and GP-RBF it changes everything: Euclidean distance on z-scored bits is dominated by the rarest substructures, which is not the fingerprint geometry the paper describes. And if `--gp-kernel tanimoto` is ever used, the Tanimoto ratio <x,y>/(||x||^2+||y||^2-<x,y>) is being evaluated on negative, continuous values — it is not a similarity in [0,1] and the denominator can vanish or go negative, so the resulting 'Tanimoto GP' number would be meaningless rather than merely different.
other_pipeline: QM9 stores ECFP4 and Avalon as packed bits (rust/src/main.rs:1602-1606; scripts/process_and_train.py:983) and unpacks them to 0/1 at read time (scripts/process_and_train.py:1380, 1326). Whether models/models.py then standardises them I did not read this session, so I cannot say whether the two pipelines differ here or share the same behaviour.

title: A failure in MHG-GNN or ChemBERTa silently deletes that representation from the whole run, while the same script raises on a missing model
what_the_code_does: Both learned representations are wrapped in `try: ... except Exception as e: print(f"    FAILED: {e} — skipping ...")`. On failure the key is simply never added to `reps`. Downstream, the experiment list is built by iterating `for rname in reps.keys()` (line ~1503), so the representation vanishes from the roster. There is no post-generation check that `rep_filter` was satisfied — in contrast to `--models`, where lines 1573-1593 raise RuntimeError with the message 'Refusing to run a partial roster' if any requested model could not be constructed.
consequence: A job launched with all six representations can exit 0, write a results CSV, and be merged into the pooled results with MHG-GNN or ChemBERTa missing for that dataset only. The representation then has unbalanced coverage across the three validation datasets, which silently biases any cross-representation aggregate and any ANOVA that assumes a full design. The failure is one line in a long log.
other_pipeline: QM9 handles the same failure the opposite way and also silently: scripts/process_and_train.py:957-959 returns `np.zeros(1024)` for a molecule MHG-GNN cannot encode, so a zero vector enters the model as if it were real features. Neither pipeline stops.

title: An unparseable molecule silently becomes an all-zero feature row on the experimental side; the Rust pipeline treats the same event as a run-stopping failure
what_the_code_does: Every static builder catches a None mol or an exception and appends `np.zeros(n_bits)` (or, for SNS, leaves the pre-allocated zero row untouched). Nothing is logged, nothing is counted, and the caller cannot tell a zero row from a genuinely featureless molecule. In practice the loaders filter unparseable SMILES upstream — load_openadmet_endpoint drops rows whose standardise_smiles returned None (line 487) — so this should be rare; I did not find a case where it fires on the current datasets.
consequence: If it ever fires, a molecule with no features gets a real label and is trained on and scored as if it were real data, and the run reports nothing. The asymmetry also means the two pipelines have opposite failure policies for the same event, so a defect that would abort a QM9 run passes silently on the validation runs.
other_pipeline: rust/src/main.rs:1563-1572: the docstring states, and the code implements, that a failure is recorded as a FeaturisationFailure and 'the run refuses to finish with any recorded failure unless explicitly permitted, so a zero fingerprint can never reach a model as if it were real features'.

title: The hERG loader does not deduplicate by canonical SMILES although the OpenADMET loaders do, so identical feature rows carry different labels
what_the_code_does: load_openadmet_endpoint collapses duplicate standardised SMILES with `sub.groupby('std_smiles').agg({endpoint_col: 'median'})` at line 490. load_chembl_herg standardises SMILES at line 509, drops nulls, and then takes `df['std_smiles'].values` and the label column straight through with no groupby. Any molecule measured more than once in ChEMBL appears as multiple rows with byte-identical features and different pKi.
consequence: hERG carries an irreducible-error floor from replicate labels that LogD and Caco-2 do not, because those were medianed. Since the study's quantity is how R2 decays as label noise is injected, a dataset that already contains replicate label noise will show a different decay curve for reasons that have nothing to do with the injected noise — and hERG is one of the three datasets the paper compares. Duplicates share a Murcko scaffold so they stay within one GroupKFold fold; this is a noise-floor problem, not a train/test leak.
other_pipeline: Not applicable — QM9 has one label per molecule.

title: create_pdv z-scores across train and test together — verified harmless because the per-fold scaler absorbs it exactly, but the code reads as a leak and would become one if that scaler were removed
what_the_code_does: create_pdv computes the 200 RDKit descriptors of DEFAULT_DESCRIPTOR_LIST (molecular.py:256-292, 200 unique names), replaces NaN/±inf with 0.0 per cell (line 967), then applies `StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)` over every molecule it was given — which, via generate_representations, is the whole dataset including the held-out fold. Because run_tree_experiment and run_neural_experiment then z-score again using training rows only, and both maps are affine, the composition equals z-scoring the raw descriptors by training statistics. I confirmed this numerically: fit-on-train of a globally-scaled matrix is allclose to fit-on-train of the raw matrix.
consequence: No numeric consequence today, and it should not be reported as a leak. Two residual notes: it is load-bearing on the per-fold scaler staying in place, and the `nan_to_num(X, nan=0.0)` at line 975 zeroes any descriptor that is constant across the whole dataset, which silently differs from zeroing one that is constant only within a fold. Recording it here so it is not re-discovered and mis-called a leak.
other_pipeline: QM9 stores continuous_pdv as raw unscaled float32 over the same 200-name DEFAULT_DESCRIPTOR_LIST (scripts/process_and_train.py:961-965, 489-491) and standardises later on the training split — the same end state. QM9's other PDV variant, `pdv`, is binarised at scripts/process_and_train.py:483 with `(pdv > 0)` and bit-packed to 25 bytes, which is a genuinely different 200-bit representation; the experimental side has no counterpart to it.

title: Two docstrings state the wrong thing about what the code produces
what_the_code_does: create_chemberta's docstring says 'Returns: np.ndarray: ChemBERTa embeddings (n_molecules, 768)'; the loaded checkpoint has hidden_size 384, so the true width is 384. create_mhg_gnn advertises `batch_size` and slices the SMILES list into batches at line 2159, but PretrainedModelWrapper.encode (~/repos/materials/models/mhg_model/load.py:51-61) loops one molecule at a time internally, so the parameter buys nothing but the progress print.
consequence: Anyone sizing a downstream layer, a PCA, or a table of representation dimensionalities from the ChemBERTa docstring gets 768 and is wrong by a factor of two. No effect on numbers already produced.
other_pipeline: On the QM9 side chemberta_fingerprint (scripts/process_and_train.py:926-931) pads or truncates to exactly 768, which matches its 768-wide model and its 3072-byte buffer, so the width there is enforced rather than assumed. Note the contrast with mhggnn_fingerprint (scripts/process_and_train.py:955), which enforces no length in the success path at all — if that model ever returned other than 1024 dims, the fixed 4096-byte record slot at rust/src/main.rs:79 would misparse every subsequent molecule.

title: KIRBy standardises the neural targets with the NOISY training SD, so the learning problem changes with the noise level -- the confound the QM9 side fixed
what_the_code_does: train_neural_regression does `y_scaler = StandardScaler(); y_train_norm = y_scaler.fit_transform(y_train)` at 867-869 and `y_val_norm = y_scaler.transform(y_val)` at 870-871. The y_train argument at the call site (line 1255) is y_noisy, the already-corrupted labels. So the divisor is sd(y_clean + epsilon) = sqrt(sd_clean^2 + dose^2), which grows with the level. Tree models in KIRBy do not scale y at all, so this touches the neural half only.
consequence: The standardised target scale shrinks as the dose rises: at the top of the Caco-2 grid (dose 0.7 log units against a label spread near 0.46) the divisor is roughly 1.8x its clean value, so the same nominal level poses a materially different optimisation problem -- fixed lr, weight decay and the absolute early-stopping tolerance (models train on the z-scale) all mean something different at each level. Predictions are inverse-transformed so the metric is on the raw scale, but the fit is not the same fit. The degradation curve, and therefore auc_norm, absorbs this.
other_pipeline: QM9 standardises with the CLEAN training mean and SD and never re-scales: generate_aggregate_stats (main.rs:1970-2005) reads train_<file_no>.mmap BEFORE preprocess_data rewrites it (call order at main.rs:2579-2593), and write_data applies (y_noisy_raw - mean)/std_dev with those clean constants (main.rs:1793-1800). models.py contains no y-scaler at all (grep for y_scaler / StandardScaler() on targets returns nothing). The two pipelines pose systematically different learning problems as the level rises.
source: Noise injection (Rust QM9 injector vs. Python NoiseInject injector, and their two callers)

title: KIRBy's noise seed keys on the POSITION of a level in the list, so a subset run does not reproduce the full run -- the docstring claims the opposite
what_the_code_does: _injector_for(condition, level_index) computes `seed = (base*1000003 + zlib.crc32(condition) + level_index*7919) & 0x7FFFFFFF` (line 1073). Every call site passes `sigma_levels.index(sigma)` -- the index of the level in whatever list was handed in, not the level's value. --sigmas (line 1993, 'Only run these sigma levels') feeds a shorter list straight through run_dataset(sigma_levels=...) (lines 1443-1446, 2042, 2086/2106/2124).
consequence: On the LogD grid [0.0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0], level 0.5 is index 3. Re-running `--sigmas 0.0 0.5 1.0` makes it index 1, so seed, epsilon and -- for outlier and grouped_wider -- the set of affected molecules all change. Rows produced by a subset run are not the rows the full run produced, and merging them into one results file mixes two different realisations under one (condition, sigma) key. The function's own docstring at 1057-1061 promises 'a run of a subset of the grid would then not reproduce the corresponding rows of a full run. The seed here depends on the condition and the level, and on nothing else' -- it depends on the level's position, which is not the same thing. Fix: key on the level value.
other_pipeline: QM9 is immune: iteration_seed = (args.random_seed ^ (iteration * 0x5DEECE66D)) & 0xFFFFFFFF (process_and_train.py:2118) is a function of the replicate only, and is passed to the binary as --seed (line 1810); main.rs:563 does StdRng::seed_from_u64(spec.seed) fresh per invocation. Any subset of the QM9 level grid reproduces the corresponding rows exactly.
source: Noise injection (Rust QM9 injector vs. Python NoiseInject injector, and their two callers)

title: grouped_shifted is scaled by three different conventions across the three implementations; they agree only because every roster pins it to Gaussian
what_the_code_does: Python _draw_grouped_shifted returns `dose * (sqrt(rho)*b[inverse] + sqrt(1-rho)*e)` where b and e come from _draw_shape -- draws at the shape's NATURAL scale, sd = unit_sd (core.py:288-299, 279-286). Delivered RMS = dose * unit_sd. Rust main.rs computes g = unit_dose(shape, scales) = unit_sd (scales are all 1.0 at line 404), solved = target / g (line 685), then `solved * (rho.sqrt()*b + (1-rho).sqrt()*w)` with b and w from draw_unit_variance (lines 703, 714-715), i.e. variance 1. Delivered RMS = target / unit_sd. The reference binary uses `target * (a*offsets + b*draw_shape)` (noise_arms.rs:256) -- Python's convention -- and its NoiseArm enum fuses shape and targeting (noise_arms.rs:30-44), so GroupedShifted has no shape field and the combination is not representable there.
consequence: For Gaussian, unit_sd = 1 and all three coincide, which is why nothing has caught it. Run `--noise-shape laplace --noise-targeting grouped_shift` (a combination main.rs:301-308 explicitly names 'grouped_shifted_laplace') and main.rs delivers target/sqrt(2) -- 29% under -- while the Python injector on the same condition delivers dose*sqrt(2), 41% over; a factor of 2 between them. Student-t at nu=5 gives 1.29x in each direction. main.rs's own realised-dose gate (lines 904-918) would abort the run, so the Rust side fails loudly; the Python injector has no runtime dose assertion in inject_verbose at all, so it would deliver the wrong amount silently. Neither cross-check can see it: the reference cannot express the condition.
other_pipeline: Latent, not currently exercised: noiseInject.CONDITIONS (core.py:56-73) and condition_roster (main.rs:968-1006) both pin grouped_shifted to Gaussian, and KIRBy's NOISE_CONDITIONS (lines 140-142) uses registry names only. Reachable today from the QM9 CLI (process_and_train.py:1815-1820 passes --noise-shape and --noise-targeting straight through).

title: The QM9 delivered-dose record writes a CSV whose rows are wider than its own header, because the level-0 manifest carries fewer parameters
what_the_code_does: record_noise_manifest flattens the JSON manifest's parameters block into param_* columns (lines 1743-1744), then appends with csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(row.keys())), writing the header only on the first call (1748-1753). Fieldnames are recomputed from each row, so no exception is raised -- the row is simply written with that call's own column set. Meanwhile main.rs:540 returns early at level <= 0, BEFORE the blocks that insert lambda/requested_group_fraction (729-739), outlier_p (740-743), n_scaffold_groups/largest_group_share_of_molecules/scaffold_lookup_miss_fraction (661-672) and censor_limit/requested_censored_fraction (602-606). I confirmed on disk that a level-0 manifest carries only {dose_units, level, shape, targeting} (scripts/noise_manifest_205052201.json and others), and reproduced the ragged output with the exact DictWriter idiom.
consequence: Because the QM9 loop runs level 0.0 first (process_and_train.py:2112), the header is written from the narrowest row. For outlier, grouped_wide, grouped_shift and censoring every subsequent level appends 2-4 extra values with no matching header cells, so pd.read_csv on <results>_noise_manifest.csv either raises or silently mis-assigns. This is the one file whose stated purpose (docstring at 1719-1724) is to record how much noise was actually delivered -- the record the redesign exists to create is unreadable for four of the five targeting rules. Gaussian/uniform is unaffected, since its parameter set does not change with level.
other_pipeline: KIRBy writes the same provenance as a fixed dict from InjectionResult.as_row() (core.py:138-159), a constant key set for every condition and level, so its provenance file is well-formed.

title: QM9 levels within a replicate share one noise draw; KIRBy levels get independent draws
line: 2112-2122 (level loop outside, seed computed inside from iteration only), with rust/src/main.rs:563 and 719-722
what_the_code_does: iteration_seed is (args.random_seed ^ (iteration * 0x5DEECE66D)) & 0xFFFFFFFF -- a function of the replicate index alone, recomputed identically at every level of the outer `for s in args.noise_level` loop. main.rs:563 seeds StdRng from it and, for uniform targeting, scale_map consumes nothing (line 402), so the epsilon at every level is the SAME standard draw multiplied by that level's solved scale: epsilon(0.6) = 2 * epsilon(0.3), exactly.
consequence: Within a QM9 replicate the whole degradation curve rides on one realisation -- a common-random-numbers design, which makes the curve unusually smooth and makes the replicate-to-replicate spread of auc_norm smaller than an independent-draw design would give. KIRBy's per-level seed (line 1073) gives independent realisations at each level, so its curves carry the full sampling wobble. The error bars on the two halves of the paper are not on the same footing, and a claim that a difference is significant on QM9 but not on the experimental sets is partly an artefact of the seeding design. Neither behaviour is wrong; they must not be compared as though they were the same design.
other_pipeline: KIRBy: independent draw per level (seed varies with level index, line 1073). QM9: one draw per replicate, rescaled across the whole grid.

title: Every QM9 job script still passes the retired --sigma / --noise-strategy flags, so no QM9 run exists under the redesigned scheme
what_the_code_does: The job script calls `python -u process_and_train.py ... --sigma 0.0 0.1 ... 1.0 --noise-strategy "$strat"`. process_and_train.py:385-394 refuses both by name: --sigma maps to --noise-level ('and note the meaning changed'), --noise-strategy maps to --noise-targeting, and the script calls parser.error(...), exiting 2 before any work.
consequence: Every QM9 job in slurm_scripts_qm9_rerun/ dies at argument parsing. The refusal is deliberate and loud, so nothing runs silently under the wrong scheme -- but it means the QM9 half of the study has not been run under the redesigned injector at all, while the experimental half has. Any table putting a QM9 number beside a LogD/Caco-2/hERG number today compares an old-scheme result (level = a per-type knob) against a new-scheme one (level = delivered dose). The job scripts and their level grids need rewriting for --noise-level/--dose-units/--noise-shape/--noise-targeting before the comparison exists.
other_pipeline: KIRBy's runner already uses the new naming throughout (NOISE_CONDITIONS at lines 140-142, NOISE_LEVELS_BY_DATASET at 169-173, CENSORING_LEVELS at 179).

title: Off-registry shape x targeting combinations get two different names in the two injectors
what_the_code_does: Python's condition property scans CONDITIONS for an exact (strategy, distribution, params) match and falls back to 'outlier/laplace'-style names when there is none (core.py:248-259). Rust's condition_name composes 'outlier_p05_laplace' for the same configuration (main.rs:309-316) and 'grouped_shifted_laplace' for a shifted one (301-308). The registry names themselves agree exactly for the eleven catalogued conditions I checked (CONDITIONS at core.py:56-73 against condition_roster at main.rs:968-1006, censoring grid [0,10,20,25,30,40,50] percent in both).
consequence: Any run outside the eleven registry entries produces results rows the two pipelines cannot be joined on, and the join failure is silent -- a filter for 'outlier_p05_laplace' simply returns nothing from the experimental side. Separately the Rust CLI keyword is grouped_wide/grouped_shift (main.rs:2417, 2427) while the emitted name and the Python strategy are grouped_wider/grouped_shifted (main.rs:223-224, core.py:75), so a job script written with the emitted name panics -- loudly -- at main.rs:2447.
other_pipeline: Both sides support the same three shapes (gaussian; student_t with nu>2; laplace) with the same unit_sd constants (main.rs:129-138 vs core.py:279-286) and the same five targeting rules with the same parameters (lambda=3, group_fraction=0.2, rho=0.62, p in {0.01,0.05,0.10}, censor side upper/lower). Censoring agrees in detail: both take the cut-point from the CLEAN training labels by linear-interpolated quantile (main.rs:342-356, 574-579 vs core.py:554-559, np.quantile default), clip strictly past it, measure the affected fraction rather than assuming it, and are excluded from the dose solver. Python additionally ships NoiseInjectorClassification (core.py:735-1006, six flip strategies) with no Rust counterpart and no dose concept; it is used only by KIRBy/tests/herg_noise_robustness.py, not by the regression pipeline.

title: A successfully computed all-zero fingerprint is not caught by the featurisation-failure gate
what_the_code_does: `prepare_ecfp4` records a failure in exactly two cases: the SMILES did not parse (`mol.is_null()`), or the bit vector is not 32 u64 chunks. A fingerprint that is computed successfully and comes back all zeros is returned as valid features. main.rs:2155-2198 then refuses to finish only if `failures` is non-empty, with the comment "a zero fingerprint would train as if it were real features" — which is precisely the case this route lets through. Because the fingerprint is path-based (finding 1), a molecule with no bonds has no paths and legitimately produces 2048 zero bits.
consequence: Measured on the first 1,500 QM9 molecules: methane, ammonia and water (SMILES 'C', 'N', 'O') get an all-zero 'ECFP4'. A real Morgan r=2 fingerprint gives all three a non-zero row. Those molecules train and are scored as if they were featurised, and every one of them presents the model with an identical, information-free input row carrying a real label. The gate the run relies on reports nothing.
other_pipeline: KIRBy returns np.zeros for molecules it cannot parse (molecular.py:311-313) and equally does not flag them, but its Morgan fingerprint never produces a spurious all-zero row for a valid small molecule.
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: `sns` computes substructure COUNTS and then bit-packs them away; KIRBy keeps the counts
what_the_code_does: `create_sort_and_slice_ecfp_featuriser` is called with `sub_counts = True`, and `ecfp_featuriser` (1003-1010) builds `sub_id_list` with each substructure repeated `count` times and sums the one-hot vectors, so the returned vector holds integer counts. `write_to_mmap` then does `np.array(sns_fp, dtype=np.uint8)` followed by `np.packbits(..., bitorder='little')`. I verified that packbits treats any non-zero as 1 (input [0,1,2,3,255] round-trips to [0,1,1,1,1]). The reader at 1174-1176 unpacks 128 bytes back to 1024 bits, so the counts are gone before storage, not at read time.
consequence: Measured on 3,000 QM9 molecules with the same generator settings: 16.1% of the non-zero SNS entries carry a count greater than 1 (max 6), and binarisation reduces 2,987 distinct count rows to 2,957 distinct binary rows — 43 molecules stop being distinguishable from another molecule. The `sub_counts=True` argument is a no-op. The same name means a count vector in one pipeline and a binary vector in the other, so any SNS comparison across datasets compares two representations.
other_pipeline: KIRBy `_transform_sns` (/Users/apunt/repos/KIRBy/src/kirby/representations/molecular.py:1240-1246) writes `features[i, idx] = count` as float32 when sub_counts is true — the counts survive. (paper.tex:203 describes SNS as producing "a binary vector", which matches the QM9 side and not KIRBy.)
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: `pdv` discards every descriptor magnitude by thresholding at zero before storage
what_the_code_does: `write_to_mmap` stores the 200 RDKit descriptors as `(pdv > 0).astype(np.uint8)` bit-packed into 25 bytes. The reader unpacks 25 bytes to 200 bits, and because 'pdv' is not in CONTINUOUS_REPS (line 121) it is never standardised and is cast to uint8 at line 1349, so the model receives 200 raw 0/1 values. The continuous values are computed (`rdkit_mol_descriptors_from_smiles`, 933-937) and thrown away at the moment of writing.
consequence: Measured on 3,000 QM9 molecules: 47 of the 200 bits are constant across the whole set (MolWt, ExactMolWt, HeavyAtomCount and similar are positive for every molecule, so their bit is always 1), and all magnitude information — the entire content of descriptors like TPSA, MolLogP, BertzCT — is reduced to a sign test. Mitigated for the headline figures, which use `continuous_pdv` (generate_paper_figures_v2.py:78, and 141 excludes 'pdv' from the ANOVA), but paper.tex:514 still reports a "PDV (binary)" uncertainty row produced by this path, and any older result labelled PDV that predates the continuous_pdv switch is this.
other_pipeline: KIRBy `create_pdv` (/Users/apunt/repos/KIRBy/src/kirby/representations/molecular.py:941-977) returns the 200 descriptors z-scored as float32. So `pdv` names a binary vector in the QM9 pipeline and a continuous one in KIRBy. The QM9 equivalent of KIRBy's PDV is `continuous_pdv` (process_and_train.py:492 write, 1194 read, 2036-2044 standardisation), and that pairing does match — including paper.tex:203's z-score description.
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: Binary and count representations are z-scored in the experimental pipeline and left raw in the QM9 pipeline
what_the_code_does: Only `CONTINUOUS_REPS = ('continuous_pdv', 'chemberta', 'mhggnn')` are standardised (2033-2044: nanmean/nanstd fitted on x_train, zero-variance columns set to 1). Everything else — ecfp4, sns, pdv, avalon, smiles, randomized_smiles — is vstacked as `np.uint8` at line 1349 and handed to the model as raw 0/1.
consequence: The same named representation reaches the models on two different scales in the two pipelines. For distance- and kernel-based models (SVM with RBF, GP with RBF) and for anything with weight decay or a shared lengthscale, a raw binary matrix and a z-scored one are different inputs: z-scoring a fingerprint amplifies rare bits by 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) and destroys the 0/1 structure. Any statement in the paper that a model's behaviour on ECFP4/SNS/Avalon carries over from QM9 to the validation datasets is comparing across this difference. (I checked the one place this could have been worse and it is not: KIRBy's GP defaults to an RBF kernel and is PDV-only, so no Tanimoto kernel is being fed z-scored input.)
other_pipeline: KIRBy standardises every representation unconditionally: StandardScaler fitted on X_train in `run_tree_experiment` (/Users/apunt/repos/KIRBy/tests/alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:1093-1095) and `run_neural_experiment` (1199-1202), which are the only two entry points (called at 1684, 1694, 1704).
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: `chemberta` is a different pretrained model in each pipeline
what_the_code_does: The QM9 pipeline loads `seyonec/ChemBERTa-zinc-base-v1` and mean-pools `outputs.last_hidden_state` over the sequence, padding/truncating the result to 768 dimensions, stored as float32 (write 506, read 1203).
consequence: The representation name 'chemberta' denotes two different pretrained encoders across the two pipelines — different pretraining corpus, different objective, different hidden width. Any joint analysis or transfer claim on ChemBERTa would be comparing unrelated embeddings. Impact on the current paper is limited: ChemBERTa is not in the Methods paragraph (paper.tex:203) and is not in EXPECTED_REPS (generate_paper_figures_v2.py:660), so no published number appears to rest on it yet.

source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: `mhggnn` never checks the encoder's output width, so a non-1024 embedding would misalign every record silently
what_the_code_does: `mhggnn_fingerprint(smiles, dimensions=1024)` returns `np.asarray(model.encode([smiles])[0], dtype=np.float32)` unchanged; `dimensions` is used only in the `except` branch. `write_to_mmap` (512) writes `mhggnn.tobytes()`, whatever length that is, while `read_smiles_data` in Rust reads a fixed `[u8; 4096]` and parse_mmap reads a fixed 4096 bytes (1212). Every other float representation enforces its width before writing — chemberta pads/truncates to 768 (902-906), and the mol2vec featuriser did the same before it was deleted.
consequence: If the pretrained wrapper ever returns anything but 1024 floats — a different pickle, a version change, a molecule the encoder handles differently — every field after mhggnn in that record is read from the wrong offset, for every molecule. The exact failure mode that the deleted `morgan` representation caused (commit cbbce0a). It would be caught downstream by the leftover-bytes check at parse_mmap (1310-1319) only if the total file length happens to disagree; a per-molecule width difference would not be caught at all.
other_pipeline: KIRBy `create_mhg_gnn` (/Users/apunt/repos/KIRBy/src/kirby/representations/molecular.py:2074-2160) loads the same PretrainedModelWrapper and the same `mhggnn_pretrained_model_0724_2023.pickle`, and vstacks whatever width comes back — no fixed-width record, so no misalignment risk there. The model itself matches between the pipelines; only the QM9 storage is width-fragile.
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: mol2vec averages substructure vectors where the published method sums them
line: 1072-1123 at git HEAD (8a5ad93/a7b16ed); deleted in the current uncommitted working tree
what_the_code_does: `mol2vec_fingerprint` builds the sentence with `mol2alt_sentence(mol, radius=1)`, sums the in-vocabulary word vectors and then divides by the count (`vec = vec / count`). The module imported `sentences2vec` (line 37) and never called it. I read the installed mol2vec source: `sentences2vec` docstring and body say "Vector is simply a sum of vectors for individual words" and it sums with no division.
consequence: The stored embedding is size-normalised, so molecular size — the strongest signal in a bag-of-substructures embedding — is divided out. That is a different representation from mol2vec as published. The paper leans on mol2vec results (paper.tex:464, 499, 523, 526, 540, 565, 567 — including "Embeddings, particularly mol2vec, are the most robust to noise"). Note also that a concurrent uncommitted edit removes mol2vec from the QM9 pipeline entirely (write path, reader, PARSEABLE_REPS, CONTINUOUS_REPS, the Rust mol2vec_buf), while generate_paper_figures_v2.py:660 still lists 'mol2vec' in EXPECTED_REPS.
other_pipeline: KIRBy `create_mol2vec` does exactly the same averaging (/Users/apunt/repos/KIRBy/src/kirby/representations/molecular.py:1625-1637). So the two pipelines agree with each other and both differ from mol2vec's own implementation — this is a naming/method-fidelity defect, not a cross-pipeline mismatch.
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: `randomized_smiles` is one-hot encoded against a vocabulary and a maximum length measured on CANONICAL SMILES
what_the_code_does: `generate_aggregate_stats` builds the token vocabulary and `max_sequence_length` by tokenizing `smiles_data.canonical_smiles`, even when the requested representation is `randomized_smiles`. `smiles_to_ohe` then encodes the randomized string against that vocabulary and truncates with `.take(max_length)`; tokens outside the vocabulary silently produce an all-zero row.
consequence: Measured on 4,000 QM9 molecules with the pipeline's own tokenizer regex: 61.8% of randomized SMILES are longer in tokens than their own canonical form, and 0.2% exceed the longest canonical training SMILES, so those molecules lose their tail tokens entirely. The vocabulary itself is safe here — QM9 canonical SMILES use 29 distinct tokens against a --max_vocab default of 30 (process_and_train.py:310) — but the length ceiling is set by the wrong string. randomized_smiles is excluded from the ANOVA anyway (generate_paper_figures_v2.py:139, "Incomplete coverage"), which bounds the damage.
other_pipeline: No equivalent in KIRBy — the experimental pipeline has no SMILES one-hot representation to compare against.
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex

title: Two latent record-misalignment routes in the Rust writer, currently unreachable on QM9
what_the_code_does: (a) The Python writer emits `struct.pack("I", 0)` for a missing randomized SMILES (process_and_train.py:471) and the Python reader always consumes 4 bytes, but the Rust re-write path writes the length prefix only inside `if let Some(randomized) = &smiles_data.randomized_smiles` (1691) — so a record with no randomized SMILES comes out 4 bytes short. (b) `read_smiles_data` rejects any record whose isomeric SMILES is under 5 characters (1426-1430) after having already consumed that field, and `write_data`'s `if let Some(...)` (1631) then continues the loop from a mid-record offset with no error.
consequence: Neither fires on QM9 as configured: `split_qm9` skips molecules with no randomized SMILES (process_and_train.py:829-830), `Chem.MolToSmiles(..., doRandom=True)` always returns a string, and PyG's QM9 stores explicit-hydrogen SMILES so the shortest is '[H]O[H]' at 7 characters (verified by loading the dataset). Route (b) is live for the Polaris/MoleculeNet path (`load_and_split_polaris`), where ordinary SMILES such as 'C', 'CCO' are under five characters and would be dropped mid-record. Route (b) also aborts rather than corrupts when it hits a TRAINING record, because read_train_labels errors on a None (1530-1541); it is the val/test splits where it degrades silently until the leftover-bytes check fires.
other_pipeline: Not applicable — KIRBy holds features in memory as numpy arrays and has no packed record format to misalign.

title: NGBoost and the GP are fitted on a smaller training set when --uncertainty is on, and both runs write into the same results file
what_the_code_does: `if args.uncertainty:` splits the validation set in half and fits on `vstack((x_train, x_val[:split_idx]))`; the `else` branch fits on `vstack((x_train, x_val))`. The calibration half is never returned to the fit. Nothing in the row written by `save_results` (scripts/utils.py:56, RESULT_COLUMNS at utils.py:23) records whether `--uncertainty` was set.
consequence: For a 10k-molecule run with a 10% validation split, an uncertainty run fits NGBoost and the GP on ~5% fewer molecules than a non-uncertainty run of the same (sigma, iteration, model, rep). The two produce different R²/RMSE and append indistinguishably to the same CSV, so a merged results file can contain two different models under one name. Compare the BNN path at 2117-2122, which carves the calibration half out of the validation set only (training is untouched), and the RF/QRF path at 1391-1392, which always merges all of validation into training — three different behaviours under one flag.
other_pipeline: KIRBy never reserves a calibration set (there is no temperature fitting anywhere in the file), so its GP and NGBoost always see the full training split. The QM9 --uncertainty rows are fitted on strictly less data than their KIRBy counterparts.

title: Temperature calibration exists only on the QM9 side, so the two pipelines' 'uncertainty' columns are different quantities
what_the_code_does: QM9 fits a scalar T by minimising Gaussian NLL over the calibration rows (`calibrate_uncertainty_simple`, utils.py:369-379) and writes `y_pred_std_calibrated = y_pred_std * T` alongside the raw std. `generate_paper_figures_v2.py` picks `y_pred_std_calibrated` first (lines 758, 3077, 3370, 3512) and only falls back to `uncertainty` when that column is absent. Grepping the whole KIRBy runner for 'calibrat' or 'temperature' returns nothing: `run_tree_experiment` (1153-1155) and `run_neural_experiment` (1256-1258) store `_tree_mean_std`/`train_neural_regression` output verbatim into the `uncertainty` column.
consequence: Every coverage and calibration number the paper reports for QM9 is post-hoc temperature-scaled; every one it reports for LogD/Caco-2/hERG is raw. Two rows of the same table under the same model name (GP, NGBoost, QRF appear on both sides) are not the same measurement. A cross-pipeline claim about calibration — 'coverage recovers at high σ', 'model X is over-confident' — is confounded by whether the row got a free scalar fitted to make it fit.
other_pipeline: KIRBy tests/alternative_data_noise_robustness.py — no calibration anywhere in the file.

title: Temperature is fitted on CLEAN held-out labels while the model was trained on noisy ones, and T is clamped to [0.1, 10]
what_the_code_does: Every QM9 calibration call passes `y_val_cal` — the validation labels decoded by `parse_mmap` as `processed_target` (scripts/process_and_train.py:1228). The Rust writer passes `apply_noise = false` for the validation split (rust/src/main.rs:2106) and records epsilon as exactly 0.0 (main.rs:1788-1789), so post-fix those labels are clean. The optimiser is `minimize_scalar(..., bounds=(0.1, 10.0), method='bounded')`, which returns a point strictly inside the interval and cannot report that it wanted to go further.
consequence: Two things. (a) The temperature absorbs the whole clean-label error of a noise-trained model, so 'calibration' at σ=1.0 means something categorically different from calibration at σ=0 — and it means something different again in the pre-fix QM9 files, where the validation labels WERE noised, so any historical temperature column is not comparable to a regenerated one. (b) When the uncalibrated std is much smaller than the residual — exactly the GP/VBLL epistemic-only case above — the NLL minimum can sit past T=10 and the returned T silently saturates near the bound, leaving `y_pred_std_calibrated` still too small with no diagnostic. Whether saturation actually occurs is checkable in the `temperature` column of a regenerated file.
other_pipeline: No counterpart in KIRBy.

title: het_gp and evidential_kernel compute a genuine per-molecule aleatoric AND epistemic term, then decline to pass either to the writer
what_the_code_does: `train_heteroscedastic_gp` computes `epistemic_std = np.sqrt(epistemic_var)` from the GP posterior (6985-6986) and `aleatoric_std = np.sqrt(noise_model(x_test_t))` — a per-molecule learned noise head (6986-6987) — then `total_std` (6990). The `save_uncertainty_values` call at 7001-7011 passes only `y_pred_std=total_std`; the `epistemic_uncertainty=` and `aleatoric_uncertainty=` keywords are omitted entirely. `train_evidential_kernel` is identical: `epistemic_std = sqrt(beta/(alpha-1))`, `aleatoric_std = sqrt(beta/(v*(alpha-1)))` at 7114-7115, and the call at 7127-7137 omits both keywords. Omitted means `np.nan` in the CSV (scripts/utils.py:288, 293).
consequence: These are the only two models in the whole roster that produce a per-molecule aleatoric term — every other decomposition path either sets aleatoric to None or broadcasts a scalar. Both write NaN into the two columns the decomposition figure and the table4 decomposition rows read (generate_paper_figures_v2.py:3472-3480). Any statement that 'the pipeline cannot separate aleatoric from epistemic per molecule' is a statement about the writer call, not about the models.
other_pipeline: KIRBy has neither model and emits no aleatoric/epistemic columns at all — its uncertainty CSV schema is sigma, sample_idx, y_true, y_pred, uncertainty (+ split/noise_type/fold/noise_scale/injected_noise in the current writer at 1766-1789).

title: The heteroscedastic head's predicted variance is sliced off and discarded at every prediction site; the one correct decomposition helper has zero callers
what_the_code_does: When `loss_name == 'heteroscedastic'` the model is built with a 2-output head — `model.fc3 = nn.Linear(params['hidden_size2'], 2)` (2172) — and then every MC loop does `if loss_name == 'heteroscedastic': output = output[:, 0:1]`, keeping the mean and dropping the predicted log-variance. The same slice is applied to the `evidential` loss (2603, 2619, 2833, 2849), which discards v, alpha and beta. `decompose_uncertainty_sampling_heteroscedastic(mean_predictions, var_predictions)` (utils.py:122) is the only helper in the file that computes aleatoric as `sqrt(var_predictions.mean(axis=0))` and total as `sqrt(epistemic**2 + aleatoric**2)`; a grep across qsar_qm_models, KIRBy and NoiseInject returns the definition line and nothing else.
consequence: Every heteroscedastic and evidential neural model reports the same quantity as a plain MC-dropout BNN — the spread of stochastic passes — so `aleatoric_uncertainty` is NaN for them (via `decompose_uncertainty_sampling`, utils.py:114) and their entire reason for existing is invisible in the output. Rows named `bnn_*_heteroscedastic` and `bnn_*_evidential` are not measuring what their names claim.
other_pipeline: KIRBy runs no heteroscedastic or evidential variant, so there is no cross-check that would have caught this.

title: Two decomposition helpers hard-code aleatoric to a constant broadcast across all molecules
what_the_code_does: `decompose_uncertainty_gp` line 164: `aleatoric = np.full_like(epistemic, np.sqrt(likelihood_noise))` — one scalar, the fitted GaussianLikelihood noise, repeated for every test molecule. `decompose_uncertainty_vbll` line 222: `aleatoric = np.full_like(epistemic, np.sqrt(learned_noise_var))` — one scalar, the VBLL layer's learned log_noise_var (models.py:1165, 1174). `decompose_uncertainty_sampling` (line 114) hard-codes `aleatoric = None` and `total = epistemic`; `decompose_uncertainty_distributional` (line 195) hard-codes `epistemic = None` and `total = aleatoric`.

Any per-molecule statistic computed from it (a Spearman ρ, a scatter, a within-group correlation) is degenerate. Across σ it is a legitimate one-number-per-run summary, but it must be plotted and described as such. Note also that models.py:1868 multiplies this constant by a temperature fitted against the epistemic-only std, which has no interpretation.

title: save_uncertainty_values writes y_true_original on the RAW label scale next to three columns on the standardised scale
line: 234-270; source of the mismatch at scripts/process_and_train.py:1155 vs 1228
what_the_code_does: `parse_mmap` decodes two targets per record: `target_value` at 1154-1155 (the raw pre-noise, pre-standardisation label, written by rust/src/main.rs before the transform) and `processed_target` at 1228-1229 (noisy where applicable, then standardised with the clean training mean/SD, rust/src/main.rs:1795-1800). These become `y_data_original` and `y_data`. Every call site passes `y_true_original=y_test_original` (raw) and `y_true_noisy=y_test` (standardised) into the same row, alongside `y_pred_mean` and `y_pred_std` which are standardised. The function papers over it by regressing `y_true_noisy` on `y_true_original` and keeping the residual as `injected_noise` (utils.py:246-254).
consequence: A reader of the CSV cannot subtract `y_pred_mean - y_true_original` — the units differ by the QM9 label mean and SD. `generate_paper_figures_v2.py` already knows and works around it (comments at 3400-3401 and 3436-3438, and a whole repair function `fix_injected_noise` at 980-1020), but the fallback branches at 3404 and 3444 still use `y_true_original` when `y_true_noisy` is absent, which would silently produce nonsense. Any ad-hoc analysis of these files that does not know the trick gets wrong errors.
other_pipeline: KIRBy writes `y_true` in raw label units and `y_pred`/`uncertainty` in the same raw units — trees and the GP are fitted on unstandardised y, and the neural path standardises internally then inverse-transforms the mean and multiplies the sd by `y_scale` (lines 953, 963), which is the correct sd rescaling. KIRBy's file is internally consistent; QM9's is not.
