title: The injected_noise column is identically zero for every QM9 test row post-fix, and the two graph paths make it zero by passing the same array twice
line: 246-254; graph call sites at models/models.py:3343 and 3544
what_the_code_does: `injected_noise` is a regression residual: `linregress(y_orig, y_noisy)` then `y_noisy - (slope*y_orig + intercept)` (utils.py:250-252). Since rust/src/main.rs:2106 and :2136 pass `apply_noise=false` for val and test, the test label IS the clean label up to the affine standardisation, so the regression is exact and the residual is 0 to float precision. Independently, `train_gnn` calls `save_uncertainty_values(predictions, total_unc, test_targets, test_targets, ...)` (3343) and `train_graph_gp` calls `save_uncertainty_values(predictions, total, test_labels, test_labels, ...)` (3544) — the same array is passed as both `y_true_original` and `y_true_noisy`, so the residual is exactly zero by construction regardless of the noise fix.
consequence: The 'does uncertainty track the injected noise' metric (`generate_paper_figures_v2.py:1033-1047`, `noise_mag = np.abs(model_data['injected_noise'])`) has no signal to find on the QM9 side and never can, because the corruption is in training and the file only holds test rows. Any regenerated QM9 unc-noise ρ will be a correlation against a zero vector. The question is answerable only from KIRBy's `split='train_oof'` rows, where `injected_noise` is the epsilon the injector actually drew (alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:1832).
other_pipeline: KIRBy writes `injected_noise: 0.0` explicitly for test rows with the comment 'test labels are never corrupted' (line 1786) and the true per-molecule epsilon for train_oof rows (line 1832) — the honest version of the same column.

title: Conformal graph model computes R² with the arguments reversed, and hard-codes the wrong z for any alpha other than 0.1
what_the_code_does: Line 4134: `metrics = calculate_regression_metrics(y_pred, y_test, logging=logging_flag)`. The signature is `calculate_regression_metrics(y_test, prediction)` (scripts/utils.py:299). MAE, MSE, RMSE and Pearson are symmetric in their arguments; `r2_score` is not — `r2_score(y_pred, y_test)` measures how well the truth explains the prediction. Line 4149: `y_pred_std = interval_width / (2 * 1.645) if alpha == 0.1 else interval_width / (2 * 1.96)`; the else branch assumes alpha=0.05 for every alpha that is not exactly 0.1, and `alpha` is tuned over [0.05, 0.2] at line 3923.
consequence: Every conformal_gin/conformal_gcn R² in the results CSV is the wrong statistic, and the function's return value (4172, `return metrics[3]`) is what Optuna maximises — so the hyperparameter search optimised the reversed R² too. The pseudo-std derived from the interval is off by a factor of 1.645/1.96 (16%) for any tuned alpha between 0.1 and 0.2, in the direction of understating uncertainty. Note the tabular conformal function does it correctly (line 3856, `calculate_regression_metrics(y_test, y_test_pred)`), so the two disagree.
other_pipeline: n/a

title: QRF and RF get no calibration set, write a null temperature, and the tuned quantile is discarded
what_the_code_does: Line 1386 draws `quantile` from Optuna (or sets 0.5) and line 1389 records it as a trial attribute, but the prediction at 1397 always asks for `quantiles=[0.16, 0.5, 0.84]` — the tuned value is never used. Lines 1391-1392 merge the whole validation set into training unconditionally, so no calibration rows exist. Line 1400's comment says 'IQR-based std estimate' while `(q84 - q16)/2` is in fact the correct ±1σ half-width for a Gaussian (the interquartile version would be q75/q25). Line 1406 sets `temperature = None` and 1407 sets `y_pred_std_calibrated = std_est`; because `y_pred_std_calibrated` is not None, `save_uncertainty_values` takes the branch at utils.py:277-278 and writes `temperature` as None — an empty cell, not 1.0.
consequence: QRF's uncertainty column is the only one in the QM9 file that is genuinely uncalibrated while still being read out of `y_pred_std_calibrated`, so a coverage table places a calibrated GP/NGBoost/BNN next to an uncalibrated QRF under one heading. The empty `temperature` cell makes that indistinguishable from a missing value rather than a deliberate no-calibration. The docstring at 1400 is wrong about the estimator's name but the arithmetic is right — do not 'fix' it.
other_pipeline: KIRBy computes the identical `(q84 - q16)/2` at tests/alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:1041-1042, so the QRF quantity itself matches across pipelines. It is the calibration status that differs.

title: conformal_hetero writes its uncertainty to a private schema that no downstream reader looks for, and the tabular conformal writer is called twice with identical arguments
what_the_code_does: `train_conformal_heteroscedastic` builds its own DataFrame with columns `y_pred_std_learned`, `y_lower_conformal`, `y_upper_conformal`, ... (7543-7553) and writes it to `<filepath>_uncertainty/uncertainty_<model>_<rep>_sigma<s>_iter<i>_file<n>.csv` (7560-7563) — not `<filepath>_uncertainty_values.csv`, which is the only name `save_uncertainty_values` produces (utils.py:244) and the only shape the figure script globs. Separately, the tabular conformal function calls `save_conformal_intervals` twice in a row at 3866-3878 and 3880-3892 with byte-identical arguments; the second call rewrites the same path (utils.py:331-333).
consequence: conformal_hetero produces a real per-molecule learned std that never reaches any table or figure — a data gap that looks like the model was never run. The duplicate call wastes a write and doubles the printed coverage line, but the file content is unchanged.

title: Blanket exception handlers turn every hard verification gate into a silently missing result row
what_the_code_does: main() wraps the entire process_and_run call in `try: ... except Exception as e: if logging: print(...); continue` (L2144-2148). A second one at L2055-2056 wraps each (rep, model) cell: `except Exception as e: print(f"Error with {rep} and {model}; more details: {e}")`. The gates added elsewhere all raise: parse_mmap's malformed-record RuntimeError (L1290-1296), its leftover-bytes check (L1305-1311), its row-count and row-width checks (L1315-1334), and process_and_run's `raise RuntimeError` on a nonzero Rust exit (L1848-1851). Every one of them lands in one of these two handlers. (Separately, `logging` at L2146 is the stdlib module imported at L30, not `args.logging`, so it is always truthy — the print does happen, but only to stdout.)
consequence: The refusal machinery cannot stop a run. A repetition whose noise plan failed its gates, whose record stream was misaligned, or whose Rust injector exited nonzero is dropped from the results CSV and the job exits 0. Cells then carry unequal numbers of repetitions with nothing on disk recording that, which biases any variance decomposition that treats repetitions as replicates and makes a silently-empty cell indistinguishable from one that was never scheduled.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: The split's notion of a scaffold group and the noise plan's notion disagree: DeepChem puts all acyclic molecules in one group, entirely into train
what_the_code_does: The split calls dc.splits.ScaffoldSplitter().split(..., 0.8/0.1/0.1) at L731-733. DeepChem's generate_scaffolds (splitters.py:1592-1605) keys on `_generate_scaffold(smiles)`, which returns the empty string for an acyclic molecule (only `None` — an unparseable SMILES — is dropped), so every acyclic molecule joins one pseudo-group; split() then fills train with the largest groups first (splitters.py:1563-1571). build_scaffold_groups, which feeds the grouped noise types, deliberately does the opposite at L419-426: `if not scaffold: scaffold = f"__acyclic__{smiles}"`, one singleton group per acyclic molecule. I ran the real path (seed 42, iteration 0, sample_size 10000): sizes are exactly 8000/1000/1000, 0 scaffold sets span more than one split, and the largest set has 1024 members — the acyclic pseudo-group — of which 1024 go to train and 0 to val or test.
consequence: 10.2% of the sample (every acyclic molecule) is structurally excluded from val and test by construction, so the held-out sets are systematically ring-containing and drawn from rarer scaffolds than training. Separately, the word "scaffold group" means two different things in the same run: grouped_wide/grouped_shift draw one offset per acyclic MOLECULE while the splitter treats all of them as one group, so the noise design's group structure is not the split's group structure.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: The Rust writer omits the randomized_smiles field entirely when it is empty, while both readers always consume 4 bytes for it
what_the_code_does: Python's writer always emits the field when the rep is enabled: a 4-byte length plus bytes, or `struct.pack("I", 0)` for missing (process_and_train.py:466-471). Rust's reader always consumes the 4-byte length when the rep is enabled (main.rs:1441-1450), and leaves `randomized_smiles = None` when it is 0. But Rust's writer is `if let Some(randomized) = &smiles_data.randomized_smiles { ...write len, write bytes... }` (main.rs:1691) — for None it writes NOTHING, not even a zero length. parse_mmap unconditionally reads 4 bytes for the field (process_and_train.py:1162-1164). Also, the OHE block at main.rs:1750 does `smiles_data.randomized_smiles.as_ref().unwrap()`, which panics on the same input.
consequence: A single record with an empty randomized SMILES makes every following record in that file 4 bytes short of where the reader expects it, and the stream cannot resynchronise. It is currently inert on QM9 only because split_qm9 skips such molecules before writing (L829-830); nothing enforces that, and the Polaris/MoleculeNet path shares this writer.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: read_smiles_data rejects a record mid-read and the callers treat the failure as end-of-data, desynchronising the stream
what_the_code_does: read_smiles_data consumes only the isomeric SMILES, then at L1426-1429 returns None if `isomeric_smiles.len() < 5 || > 300` or it contains one of four characters — leaving the rest of that record unread in the BufReader. write_data's loop body is `if let Some(smiles_data) = read_smiles_data(...)` (L1631) with no else: the index is skipped, nothing is written, and the next iteration reads from the middle of the rejected record. generate_aggregate_stats does the same at L1983 and simply omits that molecule from the mean/SD. Only read_train_labels (L1537-1547) turns None into a hard error.
consequence: Any record failing the length filter silently corrupts every record after it in the val and test files, and corrupts the standardisation constants. Currently inert for QM9: I measured the actual PyG QM9 SMILES (explicit hydrogens, e.g. '[H]C([H])([H])[H]') — minimum length 6, maximum under 300, zero records affected. It is a live hazard for any dataset with short SMILES, and it is invisible when it fires.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: The domain label byte is always written as zero, so k_domains > 1 clustering reads a constant
what_the_code_does: `if config.k_domains > 1 { writer.write_all(&[0u8])?; }` — a literal zero, with the log line hard-coded to "domain_flag: 0". parse_mmap reads the byte at process_and_train.py:1233-1236 and does nothing with it beyond printing.
consequence: The per-record domain label is a constant on both sides. Any domain-conditioned analysis reading it from the mmap sees one domain; the real labels only ever come from extract_and_cluster_for_domains. Harmless while k_domains == 1 (the default), and a byte of dead layout otherwise.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: process_and_run builds `rust_molecular_representations` and then writes the other list to the config
what_the_code_does: L1758-1760 copy args.molecular_representations and append args.domain_representation if it is missing; L1772 then writes `'molecular_representations': args.molecular_representations` into the config JSON. The augmented list is never used again. write_to_mmap is likewise driven by args.molecular_representations (L831), so the domain representation is never emitted either — the two sides are accidentally consistent.
consequence: No layout mismatch today, because neither side honours the augmented list. But the variable reads as if the Rust side is told to expect an extra representation, and the day the config line is 'fixed' to use it the writer would still not emit those bytes and every reader would shift. Dead code that looks load-bearing.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: The SMILES canonicalisation cache is read but never written, and a hit would leave `mol` as None
what_the_code_does: L779 SELECTs a canonical SMILES from smiles_db.sqlite. Grepping the whole file for INSERT/UPDATE on that table returns nothing — L132-142 create the table and the only other reference is the SELECT — so the cache is permanently empty (the on-disk file is 12 KB, schema only). If it ever were populated and 'randomized_smiles' were not requested, the `if smiles_canonical is None or 'randomized_smiles' in ...` guard at L785 would be skipped and `mol` would stay None; the sns branch re-derives it (L801-803), but nothing else does.
consequence: Inert as written. Worth knowing before anyone populates the table: a cache hit changes which molecules get a real RDKit mol object, and the featurisers that take `mol` rather than `smiles_canonical` would then silently receive None.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: file_no is derived from the wall clock and never appears in a results row
what_the_code_does: `file_no = (iteration_seed ^ int(time.time() * 1e6)) & 0xFFFFFFFF` (L2122) names the mmap files, the config, the scaffold-group JSON, the noise manifest and the per-molecule provenance CSV. save_results writes only [noise level, iteration, model, rep, n, 5 metrics, params_source, loss, spec version/hash, gp fit method, gp collapsed] (utils.py:69-72) — no file_no, no seed. record_noise_manifest does write file_no alongside iteration and noise_level into a separate *_noise_manifest.csv (L1717-1723).
consequence: A results row can only be joined to its noise provenance through (noise_level, iteration), and never directly to the file_no-named provenance CSV that holds the per-molecule y_clean/epsilon/y_written record. Two concurrent array tasks running the same (level, iteration) cell would be indistinguishable in the results file. Answering audit question 5 concretely: record position → molecule IS recoverable, but only through the provenance CSV's canonical_smiles column or by re-deriving torch.randperm from iteration_seed — the split permutation itself is never persisted.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)

title: Coverage and uncertainty-error correlation are pooled across every noise level on both sides
what_the_code_does: `model_data = rep_data[rep_data['model'] == model]` is every row for that model/rep across all 11 sigmas and all 10 iterations. `unc_err_corr`, `cov_1sigma`, `cov_2sigma` and `Mean Uncertainty` are then computed once over that whole stack. The validation mirror at line 1264-1290 does the same, grouping only by (dataset, model, rep) and pooling over sigma, over `noise_type`, and over `split`; its docstring at line 1252 even says 'Pooled across σ (matching the QM9 table)'.
consequence: One 'Coverage 1σ' number is reported for a quantity the shared spec documents as moving from 0.546 to 0.978 across noise levels (model_defaults.py, UNCERTAINTY_DEFAULTS comment). The single number is a weighted mean over the noise axis and is not the coverage of any condition that was actually run. This is an average over the very axis the study is about, and it is not disaggregated anywhere in table4.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: `fix_injected_noise` regresses across noise conditions and across splits because its grouping omits both
what_the_code_does: `required_cols = {'model','rep','sigma','iteration'}`; `group_cols = [c for c in required_cols if c in df.columns]`; then one `stats.linregress(y_orig, y_noisy)` per group. `strategy` is not in the set, and neither is `file_no` — the only column identifying which data split the row came from (written at utils.py:266). Since `required_cols` is a set literal, `group_cols` order also depends on Python's string hash seed.
consequence: All six (soon seven) noise conditions for the same model/rep/sigma/iteration are pooled into a single regression, and so are rows from different scaffold splits that happen to share an iteration index. The recovered 'normalisation transform' is then an average over conditions, and every residual it writes into `injected_noise` is wrong by that amount. The result overwrites what the writer already stored (utils.py:249-257 computes the same regression per call, correctly scoped), so the reader degrades a correct column.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: auc_norm is averaged across all six noise conditions and all representations for the headline cross-dataset figures
what_the_code_does: `model_ds_c = val_auc_df.pivot_table(values='auc_norm', index='model', columns='dataset', aggfunc='mean')`, `qm9_means_c = qm9_auc_df.groupby('model')['auc_norm'].mean()`, and `qm9_mn/ext_mn = ...groupby('model')['auc_norm'].mean()`. `auc_df` from `calculate_robustness` (line 1818) has one row per (model, rep, strategy), so `groupby('model').mean()` collapses 6 strategies × 5 reps into one number. The same pattern drives `compute_icc_and_redundancy` at line 2453 (`overall_auc = mean_auc.groupby(['model','rep'])['auc_norm'].mean()`).
consequence: Panel A and Panel B of the combined validation figure, and the model×dataset heatmap, report a robustness value no configuration has. Line 2453 is worse than cosmetic: the strategy-averaged correlations it produces are what justify `ANOVA_MODELS_EXCLUDE` (line 129-133, 'qrf: Redundant with rf (rho = 0.996)'), so a model is dropped from the ANOVA on the basis of an average across the six conditions.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: Four models never record which parameters produced their rows
what_the_code_does: `train_svm_model` (1436-1477) sets `params_source` at 1438/1444/1459/1462 but calls `save_results(args.filepath, s, iteration, 'svm', rep, args.sample_size, metrics)` at 1474 without it. The same omission is in `train_xgboost_model` (sets at 1586-1662, saves at 1632), `train_lgb_model` (sets at 1639-1662, saves at 1674) and `train_rnn_variant_model` (sets at 2931-2949, saves at 2990). `save_results` defaults `params_source='default'` (utils.py:29).
consequence: For SVM, XGBoost, LightGBM and the RNN variants the `params_source` column reads 'default' even when the run used `--use-best-params` or Optuna-tuned values. A CSV containing a mixture of tuned and default fits for those four models is indistinguishable, and the figure script has no way to separate them (it never reads the column — `grep params_source` on the figure script returns zero hits).
other_pipeline: KIRBy has no per-model parameter source; it stamps `spec_version`/`spec_hash` on every row from the shared spec (line 1758-1760), which is the same guarantee expressed differently.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: `sample_size` means the total sample for most models but the test-set size for two graph models
what_the_code_does: `save_results(args.filepath, s, iteration, model_name, 'graph', len(test_targets), metrics)` — the sixth positional argument is `n`, which `save_results` writes into the `sample_size` column (utils.py:69-70). Line 3540 does the same with `len(test_labels)` for `graph_gp`. Every other call site passes `args.sample_size` (the `-n` flag, 10000 in the re-run scripts), including the other graph path at line 4145.
consequence: Within one QM9 results file the `sample_size` column holds 10000 for most rows and roughly 1000 for `train_gnn`/`graph_gp` rows. Nothing downstream reads the column today, but any filter or join on it, and any table that reports dataset size per model, is wrong by an order of magnitude for those two models.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: Provenance columns written by both pipelines are read by neither the figure script nor anything else
what_the_code_does: `grep -n "spec_version\|spec_hash\|gp_collapsed\|gp_fit_method\|params_source\|file_no\|temperature"` over the whole figure script returns no hits for any of them. `save_results` writes `spec_version`, `spec_hash`, `gp_fit_method` and `gp_collapsed` (utils.py:69-72); KIRBy writes `spec_version`, `spec_hash`, `gp_fit_method` plus 17 realised-dose columns (lines 1741-1762); `save_uncertainty_values` writes `file_no` and `temperature` (utils.py:266, 278/282).
consequence: Three concrete losses. (1) `gp_collapsed` marks a GP fit that predicted a constant — models.py:1878-1881 records it precisely so a failed fit is not read as a bad representation — but the figure script averages collapsed fits into auc_norm alongside real ones. (2) `spec_version`/`spec_hash` are never filtered on, and the model_defaults change log states that 1.1.0 'INVALIDATES every existing forest and quantile-forest result'; rows written under 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 are pooled and averaged by `calculate_robustness` with no guard. (3) `gp_fit_method` distinguishes the botorch fit from the Adam fallback, i.e. two different fits, also pooled.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: The QM9 noise manifest is keyed on a column the results file does not have, and its header is fixed by whichever condition wrote first
what_the_code_does: `record_noise_manifest` builds a row keyed by `iteration`, `file_no`, `noise_level` plus the manifest's own fields plus `param_*` entries, and appends with `csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(row.keys()))`, writing the header only when the file is new. The `param_*` set is condition-dependent: rust/src/main.rs:728-745 inserts `{lambda, requested_group_fraction}` for grouped_wide, `{group_variance_share}` for grouped_shift, `{outlier_p, lambda}` for outlier and nothing for uniform/censoring.
consequence: Two problems. First, traceability: the manifest is keyed by `file_no`, but `file_no` is not in RESULT_COLUMNS, so a results row can only be joined to its manifest through (iteration, noise_level), and the manifest carries no model or rep. Second, appending a second targeting to the same manifest path raises `ValueError: dict contains fields not in fieldnames` from DictWriter — which is called at line 1848, outside the per-model try/except at line 2055, so it aborts the job; a targeting with FEWER params instead blank-fills and the header silently stops describing the rows.
other_pipeline: KIRBy puts the whole realised-dose provenance inline on each result row (`unit_dose_g`, `solved_scale`, `realised_dose_label_units`, `mean_epsilon`, `effective_n`, `seed`, ... at lines 1741-1757), so no join is needed and no header can drift.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: A QM9 uncertainty row cannot be traced to a molecule; a KIRBy one can
what_the_code_does: `save_uncertainty_values` writes `'sample_idx': i`, the loop position within that call's test array, plus `file_no`. `file_no` is generated at process_and_train.py:2122 as `(iteration_seed ^ int(time.time() * 1e6)) & 0xFFFFFFFF` — a fresh value per repetition, and the mmap files it names are deleted in the `finally` block at line 2058-2060. No SMILES, no dataset index and no scaffold id is written. `parse_mmap` can return canonical SMILES (`return_smiles`, line 1109-1116) but only the feature-dump path asks for it.
consequence: `sample_idx = 7` in iteration 0 and `sample_idx = 7` in iteration 1 are different molecules, and there is no way to find out which. Any per-molecule question on QM9 — is it always the same molecules that the model is uncertain about, do uncertain molecules share a scaffold — is unanswerable from the files, and the figure script's dedup on `sample_idx` (line 939-946) is merging rows that are not the same molecule.
other_pipeline: KIRBy writes `'mol_idx': int(test_idx[i])` alongside `sample_idx` (line 1772-1782) with a comment stating exactly why, and preserves it through GP subsampling via `gp_row_idx` (line 1636-1645).
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: `retention_0.5` and `retention_1.0` are silently NaN for two of the three validation datasets

title: rmse, mae and the mean-uncertainty columns are in different units on the two sides while sharing names
what_the_code_does: KIRBy inverse-transforms neural predictions back to raw label units (`_to_raw`, line 952-954) and rescales the predictive std by `y_scale` (line 963), and trains tree models on raw `y` throughout; `compute_metrics` (line 1315-1326) then computes r2/rmse/mae in raw log units. QM9 standardises every label in Rust (`property_value = (property_value - mean) / std_dev`, rust/src/main.rs:1798-1799) and never inverts, so `calculate_regression_metrics` (utils.py:74-89) returns rmse/mae in standardised units and `save_uncertainty_values` stores `y_true_noisy`, `y_pred_mean` and the stds in standardised units.
consequence: `rmse` and `mae` mean different things in the two all-results files. More visibly, `table4_uncertainty_metrics.csv` reports 'Mean Uncertainty' and 'Mean |Error|' in label SDs while `table_validation_uncertainty.csv` reports them in log units, and the second table's docstring (line 1249-1256) says it 'Mirrors the QM9 uncertainty metrics'. Coverage, being dimensionless, is comparable; those two columns are not. The figure script's docstring at line 1181-1185 correctly notes the validation side is in raw units but nothing acts on the difference.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back

title: The uncertainty loader globs the same files twice, and its dedup key omits file_no

The second pattern is a strict superset of the first, so every `uncertainty_*` file is read and concatenated twice. title: The CV scaffold string carries stereochemistry, so enantiomers are split across folds — 4.35% of LogD test molecules have an ECFP4 vector identical to a training molecule's
what_the_code_does: get_scaffold returns Chem.MolToSmiles(core, canonical=True). RDKit's MolToSmiles defaults to isomericSmiles=True, so the scaffold key includes @/@@ and E/Z. assign_scaffold_groups then maps that string to a group id, and those ids are what GroupKFold holds out (line 1618/1622). Stereoisomers of one Bemis-Murcko framework therefore land in DIFFERENT groups and can be split between train and test. Measured this session on the cached data: LogD 2387 chirality-aware groups vs 2245 chirality-blind (142 frameworks split), and 368 LogD molecules (7.3%), 79 Caco-2 (3.7%), 36 hERG (2.5%) sit in a framework family that straddles more than one fold. create_ecfp4 (src/kirby/representations/molecular.py:295-322) builds GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=2048) with includeChirality left at False, so those stereoisomers are bit-identical.
consequence: Measured with the pipeline's own featuriser and its own fold geometry: 219/5039 LogD test rows (4.35%), 54/2161 Caco-2 (2.50%) and 17/1415 hERG (1.20%) have an ECFP4 vector bit-identical to a molecule in their own fold's training set. Under a chirality-blind scaffold key those fall to 0.08%, 0.09% and 0.00%. Baseline R2 on the fingerprint representations is inflated by memorised rows, and inflated unequally across the three datasets — which is exactly the axis the paper compares (paper.tex:547, 556). The module's own docstring (lines 33-36) claims the split 'Holds out entire scaffold groups per fold / Tests generalization to novel chemotypes'; for 7.3% of LogD it does not.
other_pipeline: QM9 groups chirality-blind on both of its paths: scripts/process_and_train.py:408 uses MurckoScaffoldSmiles(smiles=smiles, includeChirality=False), and the split itself is deepchem's ScaffoldSplitter, whose _generate_scaffold (deepchem 2.8.0, splits/splitters.py) calls MurckoScaffoldSmiles(mol=mol, includeChirality=include_chirality) with include_chirality defaulting to False. Same claimed 'Murcko scaffold split', different grouping rule.
source: Data preprocessing and splitting on the experimental side (KIRBy/tests/alternative_data_noise_robustness.py)

title: The validation set is a contiguous alphabetical block of SMILES; 19% of every dataset never enters any model's training set
what_the_code_does: n_val = len(train_idx) // 5; val_idx_local = np.arange(n_val); train_idx_local = np.arange(n_val, len(train_idx)). This takes the FIRST 20% of train_idx. sklearn returns train_idx in ascending index order, and the datasets are ordered alphabetically by canonical SMILES (load_openadmet_endpoint line 491 groups by std_smiles, which sorts; the hERG cache was written by the same kind of groupby at line 461). I confirmed the ordering: LogD and Caco-2 arrays are exactly sorted ascending. So the validation split is the alphabetically-earliest slice of the training rows, and the training remainder is everything after it. Measured on LogD fold 0: 413 of 806 validation SMILES begin 'CN', while the training remainder's commonest prefixes begin at 'Cc'; halogen-bearing fraction 0.25 (val) vs 0.33 (train). Caco-2 fold 0: 0.28 vs 0.39. hERG fold 0: mean heavy-atom count 34.3 (val) vs 31.2 (train). The carve is also not scaffold-aware: 68-73% of validation molecules on LogD/Caco-2 (33-41% on hERG) share a scaffold with a training molecule. Across all five folds, 981/5039 LogD (19.5%), 419/2161 Caco-2 (19.4%) and 260/1415 hERG (18.4%) molecules are in NO fold's training set.
consequence: Every model — trees, kernels and nets alike — trains on 64% of the dataset rather than 80%, and the ~19% that is never trained on is a chemically coherent alphabetical band, not a random sample, so the loss does not average out across folds. Neural early stopping is judged on a slice that is both chemically skewed and scaffold-overlapping with training (interpolation), while the test set is scaffold-disjoint (extrapolation). Baseline R2 — the denominator of every retention and auc_norm number — is depressed by the smaller, truncated training set. The file already knows this is wrong: the inner cross-fitting path at line ~1300 carves its validation from the inner fold's own rows precisely because 'reusing the outer validation set would early-stop against molecules sharing scaffolds with the rows being scored (26-42% overlap on the real datasets)'. The outer carve was left as-is.
other_pipeline: QM9 merges validation back into training for seven model families before fitting — models/models.py:1391 (RF/QRF), 1464 (SVM), 1511 (NGBoost), 1623 (XGBoost), 1665 (LightGBM), 1820 and 3722 (GP) — on an 80/10/10 deepchem scaffold split (scripts/process_and_train.py:598), so those models see 90% of QM9 against 64% of each experimental set under the same model name. Its validation split is also scaffold-disjoint, where the experimental one is not.
source: Data preprocessing and splitting on the experimental side (KIRBy/tests/alternative_data_noise_robustness.py)

title: The SNS featuriser is fitted on the whole dataset, test folds included
line: 1375 (called from 1518, before the CV loop at 1622)

title: Label standardisation for the neural models is fitted on the NOISY training labels — the exact confound QM9 fixed in Rust
what_the_code_does: train_neural_regression fits y_scaler = StandardScaler() on its y_train argument. run_neural_experiment passes y_noisy there (lines 1272-1273: train_neural_regression(X_train, y_noisy, X_val, y_val_used, X_test, ...)), so the target mean and spread used for z-scoring move with the noise level. Predictions and uncertainties are inverse-transformed back to raw units at lines 963-966, so R2 itself is unaffected by the affine map; what moves is the scale the MSE/ELBO, the early-stopping comparison (best_val, tolerance = NEURAL_DEFAULTS['training']['improvement_tolerance']) and the effective learning rate all live on. Tree and kernel models get no label standardisation at all here — they see raw log units.
consequence: For the six neural models the optimisation problem is rescaled at every noise level, so the degradation curve is not measured on a fixed footing along its own x-axis, and it is measured on a different footing from its QM9 counterpart. Separately, because the trees/kernels see raw log labels here and z-scored labels on QM9, SVR's unpinned epsilon (sklearn default 0.1; models/model_defaults.py:127-135 pins only C, gamma, kernel) is 0.10 label-SD on QM9 but 0.22 on Caco-2 (label SD 0.445), 0.084 on LogD (1.190) and 0.109 on hERG (0.914); the GP's init_noise=1e-3 and outputscale=1.0 are likewise priors stated in units of a label whose SD is 1 on QM9 and 0.445-1.19 here. The comment at lines 1550-1553 asserting that SVM 'is the same model on QM9 and on the validation datasets' is therefore false as written. RMSE and MAE are also in different units between the pipelines (QM9 scores against the normalised target, models.py:1469), so any table putting them side by side compares unlike quantities; R2 is safe.
other_pipeline: QM9 standardises the label with the CLEAN training mean and spread and does so for every model, in Rust: rust/src/main.rs:1793-1799, whose comment reads 'Standardising with the noisy spread (the old behaviour) moved the target scale with the noise level, so "the same amount of noise" meant something different at every level (RERUN_PLAN.md §2.4).' The fix was applied on the QM9 side only.

title: The hERG dataset is fetched live from ChEMBL with no version pin, and the cache directory is a relative path

Because ChEMBL grows, two runs launched from different directories, or at different times, can train on different datasets. title: Caco-2 log transform clips non-positive efflux ratios to 1e-10, producing a label of -10 that the finiteness filter cannot catch
what_the_code_does: labels_arr = np.log10(np.clip(labels_arr, 1e-10, None)) followed by valid = np.isfinite(labels_arr) and a filter on it. Clipping to 1e-10 rather than dropping means any efflux ratio <= 0 becomes exactly -10.0, which is finite, so the isfinite filter keeps it. I checked the cached file: the Caco-2 efflux column has min 0.26 and zero non-positive values in both openadmet_train.csv and openadmet_raw.csv, so nothing is clipped today. (LogD has 260 non-positive values but is loaded with log_transform=False, so it is untouched.)
consequence: Latent, not live. The Caco-2 label mean is 0.293 with SD 0.445; a single clipped molecule would enter at -10, i.e. 23 SD below the mean, and would move the R2 of every Caco-2 row in the study. It survives only because the current extraction happens to contain no zero.

title: assign_scaffold_groups puts every acyclic molecule in one CV group; the sibling function fixes this for noise but not for splitting

I counted acyclic molecules in all three datasets: 0, 0 and 0.

It would matter on any dataset containing acyclic compounds; QM9 is 32.2% acyclic per the assign_noise_groups docstring, and QM9's own grouping already gives them singletons (scripts/process_and_train.py:417-418).

title: hERG deduplication runs on the raw ChEMBL SMILES, before standardisation, and standardisation never neutralises charges
what_the_code_does: fetch_chembl_herg_ki groups by the raw canonical_smiles column, takes the median pchembl and drops high-variance compounds, then caches. load_chembl_herg applies standardise_smiles afterwards (line 512) and never re-deduplicates, so two ChEMBL records whose raw SMILES differ but which standardise to the same molecule would survive as two rows with two labels. standardise_smiles itself (298-312) keeps the largest fragment but does not neutralise charges or normalise tautomers, despite the docstring saying 'remove salts', so a free acid and its salt's anion would not collapse either. Measured on the cached file: 1,415 rows, 1,415 unique standardised SMILES, 24 rows whose SMILES changed under standardisation, 0 collisions; 3 net-charged molecules in LogD, 0 in Caco-2, 3 in hERG, and running an RDKit Uncharger over all three datasets reveals 0 additional duplicates. The OpenADMET loader does it in the right order (standardise at 486, then group by std_smiles at 491).
consequence: Latent on the current data, not live. It becomes real the moment the ChEMBL cache is refreshed (see the unpinned-fetch finding), because duplicate rows would then carry conflicting labels into the same scaffold group.
other_pipeline: QM9 canonicalises with Chem.MolToSmiles(mol, isomericSmiles=False) (scripts/process_and_train.py:646), i.e. stereochemistry-stripped, where the experimental side keeps stereochemistry — a further reason the two 'canonical SMILES' are not the same key.

Because the per-fold scaler re-centres on the training rows, the composition is algebraically identical to standardising raw descriptors per fold, so it leaks nothing net — but it is a dataset-wide fit sitting in front of a CV loop, and it is harmless only by accident.

title: QM9 bit-packs the Sort-and-Slice substructure COUNTS; the experimental pipeline keeps them as counts
what_the_code_does: QM9 builds the featuriser with sub_counts=True (process_and_train.py:617), so ecfp_featuriser(mol) returns counts — and then write_to_mmap does sns_fp_array = np.array(sns_fp, dtype=np.uint8); sns_fp_packed = np.packbits(sns_fp_array, bitorder='little') and stores 128 bytes, read back with np.unpackbits into 1024 bits at line 1184. packbits treats any nonzero as 1, so the counts are discarded. KIRBy's _transform_sns writes the integer counts into a float32 array and keeps them.

'SNS' names a binary presence vector on QM9 and a substructure-count vector on the three experimental datasets. Combined with the finding above (SNS is no longer standardised on the experimental side), the SNS columns now reach an RBF SVM as unscaled raw counts on one side and raw bits on the other.

title: The label the models are fitted on is z-scored for every model on QM9 and raw log units for the tree/kernel half on the experimental side — so `SVM`, `GP`, `NGBoost`, `rmse` and `mae` all mean different things
file: models/model_defaults.py:130-134 pins SVR to C=1.0, gamma='scale', kernel='rbf' and leaves `epsilon` at the sklearn default 0.1. Measured label SDs this session: LogD 1.1906, Caco-2 log10 0.4449, hERG 0.9147, QM9 1.000 by construction. So the SVR dead zone is 0.100 label SD on QM9, 0.084 on LogD, 0.225 on Caco-2 and 0.109 on hERG — 2.25x wider on Caco-2 than on QM9 under one model name. The GP's GP_DEFAULTS likelihood_noise 1e-3 and outputscale 1.0 (model_defaults.py:144-146) and NGBoost's lr 0.01 over 500 stages are stated relative to a unit-variance target on one side and an arbitrary-variance one on the other.
what_the_code_does: QM9: rust/src/main.rs:1793-1800 standardises the target with the CLEAN training mean and spread for EVERY split and every model, before any model sees it. models/models.py contains no target scaler (`grep StandardScaler|y_scaler` returns nothing). So all QM9 models fit a unit-variance label, and calculate_regression_metrics returns rmse/mae in standardised units.

Baseline R² and the shape of the degradation curve for SVM, GP and NGBoost differ between pipelines for this reason alone. Separately, `rmse` and `mae` share a column name while being in label SDs on one side and log units on the other, so any table putting them side by side compares unlike quantities. R² and coverage, being dimensionless, are safe.
source: cross-pipeline

title: The neural target scaler uses the NOISY label spread on the experimental side and the CLEAN spread on QM9 — the confound QM9 fixed, still live in KIRBy
file: Read both. Measured clean SDs: LogD 1.1906, Caco-2 0.4449, hERG 0.9147. At the top of the Caco-2 grid (dose 0.7 against SD 0.4449) the divisor is sqrt(1 + (0.7/0.4449)²) = 1.86x its clean value.
what_the_code_does: QM9: rust/src/main.rs:1793-1800, whose own comment reads: 'Standardise with the CLEAN training mean and spread. Standardising with the noisy spread (the old behaviour) moved the target scale with the noise level, so "the same amount of noise" meant something different at every level.'
other_pipeline: experimental: KIRBy alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:867-872 fits `y_scaler = StandardScaler()` on its `y_train` argument, and run_neural_experiment passes `y_noisy` there (:1272-1274). Since the injected noise is independent of the label, the divisor is sqrt(sd_clean² + dose²), which rises monotonically with the level. `y_scale` is then used to rescale the predictive std back to label units at :963.
consequence: For the six experimental neural models the optimisation problem is rescaled at every noise level — a fixed lr, the absolute early-stopping tolerance (NEURAL_DEFAULTS improvement_tolerance 0.0 on a mean loss) and the effective regularisation all mean something different at each point on the x-axis, and the reported per-molecule uncertainty carries a mechanical sqrt(1+(dose/sd_clean)²) inflation before the model has done anything. The QM9 neural rows carry none of it. Any claim that 'the Bayesian nets' intervals widen as noise rises', and any experimental coverage-at-1σ/2σ number for BNN-Full, VBLL-Full, MLP-BNN-Full or MLP-VBLL-Full, is partly this factor and is not comparable with its QM9 counterpart.
source: cross-pipeline

title: 'The training set' is 90% of the data on QM9 and 64% on the experimental side, for the same seven model families
file: Read all seven vstack sites and the n_val carve this session. Nothing in the results row records which regime produced it — RESULT_COLUMNS (utils.py:23-26) has `sample_size` but no train-size field, and QM9's graph paths write the TEST size into `sample_size` (models.py:3338, :3540) while every other site writes args.sample_size, so that column is not usable as a check either.
what_the_code_does: QM9: Seven families unconditionally stack the validation split back onto training before fitting: models/models.py:1391 (RF/QRF), :1464 (SVM), :1623 (XGBoost), :1665 (LightGBM), :1506/:1511 (NGBoost), :1815/:1820 (Gauche GP), :3722 (conformal). On the 80/10/10 deepchem scaffold split (process_and_train.py:743) that is 90% of the sample.
other_pipeline: experimental: KIRBy alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:1633-1637 carves the first fifth of each outer fold's training rows off as validation (`n_val = len(train_idx)//5`) and hands only the remaining rows to run_tree_experiment (:1702-1712). The carve-out is never returned. With 5-fold GroupKFold that is 0.8 x 0.8 = 64% of the dataset, and the ~19% never used for training is a contiguous block of the array rather than a random sample.
consequence: The same named model is fitted on materially different amounts of data in the two studies, and training-set size is itself a determinant of label-noise robustness — more data averages more injected noise away. Baseline R² on the experimental side is depressed relative to what the same estimator would give, and since baseline R² is the denominator of every retention and auc_norm number, the whole cross-pipeline robustness comparison carries an uncontrolled sample-size term. This also collides with the supervisor's standing query about the 'smaller datasets' claim in Fig 8.
source: cross-pipeline

title: 'Scaffold split' groups chirality-blind on QM9 and chirality-aware on the experimental side, so stereoisomers are split across folds there
file: Measured on the cached datasets this session with the pipeline's own function: LogD 2387 chirality-aware groups vs 2245 blind (142 frameworks split across group ids, 894 molecules whose scaffold key changes), Caco-2 1069 vs 1038 (31 frameworks, 261 molecules), hERG 768 vs 750 (18 frameworks). create_ecfp4 leaves includeChirality at False (molecular.py:308), so those stereoisomers are bit-identical in the fingerprint. Acyclic count is 0 in all three datasets, so the separate acyclic-grouping divergence is latent there.
what_the_code_does: QM9: scripts/process_and_train.py:743 uses `dc.splits.ScaffoldSplitter()`, whose `_generate_scaffold` calls `MurckoScaffoldSmiles(mol=mol, includeChirality=include_chirality)` with include_chirality defaulting to False (deepchem splits/splitters.py:1277, :1318, called bare at :1599). The QM9 noise grouping is explicitly chirality-blind too (process_and_train.py:428, `includeChirality=False`).
other_pipeline: experimental: KIRBy alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:320, get_scaffold: `return Chem.MolToSmiles(core, canonical=True)`. RDKit's MolToSmiles defaults to isomericSmiles=True, so the scaffold key carries @/@@ and E/Z. assign_scaffold_groups (:327-333) maps that string to the group id GroupKFold holds out (:1618-1622).
consequence: Stereoisomers of one Bemis-Murcko framework land in different CV groups and can therefore be split between train and test, giving bit-identical fingerprint rows on both sides of the split — memorised rows inflating baseline R² on the fingerprint representations, and inflating it unequally across the three datasets (LogD worst, hERG least). The module docstring's claim that the split 'Holds out entire scaffold groups per fold / Tests generalization to novel chemotypes' does not hold for those molecules, and the QM9 side, which is genuinely chirality-blind, has no equivalent inflation. The phrase 'Murcko scaffold split' in the paper describes two different grouping rules.
source: cross-pipeline

title: `pdv` names a 200-bit sign vector on QM9 and 200 continuous descriptors on the experimental side; the matching pair is `continuous_pdv` / `PDV`, and even that pair handles non-finite descriptors differently
file: The descriptor lists are identical: I diffed DEFAULT_DESCRIPTOR_LIST in scripts/process_and_train.py:74 against KIRBy molecular.py:256 — 200 entries each, same names, same order, zero difference. generate_paper_figures_v2.py:1077 correctly maps 'PDV' -> 'continuous_pdv', so the headline figures pair the right objects. But non-finite handling diverges: KIRBy does per-cell `np.nan_to_num(desc, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)` at molecular.py:967 BEFORE scaling, while QM9 returns raw values (process_and_train.py:944-948) into a nanmean/nanstd block (process_and_train.py:2063-2072). I ran that arithmetic: one +inf in a column gives nanmean=inf and nanstd=nan, the `x_std[x_std==0]=1.0` guard does not catch nan, and the subsequent np.nan_to_num zeroes the ENTIRE column for every molecule rather than the one cell.
what_the_code_does: QM9: scripts/process_and_train.py:496-497: `pdv_binary = (pdv > 0).astype(np.uint8)` then `np.packbits(...)`, 25 bytes, unpacked to 200 bits at :1214. Not in CONTINUOUS_REPS (:133), so it is never standardised. The magnitudes are computed by rdkit_mol_descriptors_from_smiles (:944-948) and thrown away at the moment of writing. `continuous_pdv` (:1194 region) keeps the same 200 values as float32.
other_pipeline: experimental: KIRBy has no binary counterpart. create_pdv (molecular.py:955-977) returns the 200 descriptors z-scored as float32 — that is the object named `PDV` throughout the experimental roster.
consequence: Two costs. (1) paper.tex still reports a 'PDV (binary)' uncertainty row produced by the QM9 sign-vector path, and any older result labelled PDV that predates the continuous_pdv switch is that object — a comparison of 'PDV' across the two pipelines, or of `pdv` against `continuous_pdv` within QM9, is a comparison between a sign vector and a descriptor vector, not two encodings of the same information. (2) Within the correctly-paired continuous_pdv/PDV, a single infinite descriptor silently deletes a whole feature column on QM9 and a single cell on the experimental side.
source: cross-pipeline

title: The SNS feature vocabulary is fitted on training molecules only on QM9 and on the whole dataset, held-out folds included, on the experimental side
file: Read both call orderings this session and confirmed generate_representations runs before the fold loop.
what_the_code_does: QM9: scripts/process_and_train.py:625-632 builds `mols_train` from `train_idx` ONLY and passes just those molecules to create_sort_and_slice_ecfp_featuriser; val and test are then transformed with the training-fitted featuriser. The same at :757-762 on the other branch.
other_pipeline: experimental: KIRBy alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:1375: `reps['SNS'], _ = create_sns(smiles_list, return_featurizer=True)` on the FULL SMILES array, called from run_dataset at :1518 — a hundred lines before GroupKFold splits anything at :1618. create_sns is a fitted transform: molecular.py:1195-1202 counts how many of the molecules it is given contain each circular substructure and keeps the top 1024 as the feature columns. Its own docstring says 'Must be fitted on training data first'.
consequence: Which 1024 substructures become the experimental SNS basis is chosen with every fold's held-out molecules in view — a transductive feature-selection leak affecting every SNS row of all three datasets and all seven conditions, and absent from the QM9 SNS rows the paper places beside them. It is unsupervised so the effect is modest, but it is asymmetric: only SNS has it, only on one pipeline. So 'SNS' names two different fitting PROTOCOLS on top of naming two different dtypes.
source: cross-pipeline

title: Model names in the experimental uncertainty FILENAMES are hyphen-stripped, so the four Bayesian/variational models never map to their QM9 names
file: generate_paper_figures_v2.py:1211 recovers the model from the filename (`model_raw, rep_raw = parts[0], '_'.join(parts[1:])`) and then maps it through val_model_map at :1062-1075, which is keyed on the HYPHENATED names 'BNN-Full', 'VBLL-Full', 'MLP-BNN-Full', 'MLP-VBLL-Full'. 'BNNFull' is not a key, so `.fillna(df['model'].str.lower())` at :1092 yields 'bnnfull'. Meanwhile all_results.csv keeps the hyphens in its `model` column and maps correctly.
what_the_code_does: QM9: QM9 stores the model name inside the CSV, in the `model` column written by save_results (scripts/utils.py:23-26), so the reader never has to parse it out of a path.
other_pipeline: experimental: KIRBy alternative_data_noise_robustness.py:1435: `fname = f"{model_name.replace('-', '')}_{rep_name.replace('-', '')}_uncertainty_values.csv"`. 'BNN-Full' becomes 'BNNFull', 'MLP-VBLL-Full' becomes 'MLPVBLLFull'.
consequence: In table_validation_uncertainty.csv the four models appear as bnnfull / vbllfull / mlpbnnfull / mlpvbllfull, while the same models in table_validation_auc.csv appear as dnn_bnn_full / dnn_vbll / mlp_bnn_full / mlp_vbll. Any join or side-by-side reading of the two validation tables silently drops all four — and these are exactly the models the paper's BNN-family comparison (fig4/fig5) depends on.
source: cross-pipeline
